---
title: "The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down"
subtitle: "How teams buy and sell seconds, why the last two minutes of a half look like a different sport, and how fourth down went from a punting down to a decision"
description: "Game management end to end: what each kind of play costs a hurrying offense in game-clock seconds (from nflverse data); the out-of-bounds clock rule; the two-minute drill (sideline throws, the spike and why it isn't grounding, timeouts, the 10-second runoff); the four-minute offense, kneel-down arithmetic and the victory formation; end-of-half choices (field-goal range, the Hail Mary, the prevent defense, the intentional safety and the fair-catch kick); fourth-down and two-point heuristics and the 2018-2025 aggression shift, with go-rate charts; and the 2022 playoff and 2025 regular-season overtime rules and their strategy. Film rooms: Super Bowl LVIII, the Chiefs' 2015 and Eagles' 2004 slow drives, the Lions' 2023 NFC Championship, Falcons-Lions 2017, Patriots-Broncos 2003 and the Chargers' 2024 fair-catch kick."
glossary:
  "Two-minute drill": "The hurry-up offense a team runs when it needs to score with little time left in a half, usually the last two minutes: no huddle, plays called in pairs, throws to the sideline so receivers can step out of bounds, and timeouts and spikes used to stop the clock."
  "Spike": "A quarterback taking the snap under center and immediately throwing the ball straight into the ground. It is a legal incomplete pass, not intentional grounding, and it stops the clock at the price of a down."
  "10-second runoff": "Ten seconds taken off the game clock as a penalty when, after the two-minute warning of either half, the offense stops the clock illegally (a foul, intentional grounding, an illegal pass) or a replay reversal turns a stopped clock into a running one. The offense can avoid a foul-caused runoff by using a timeout, and either half can end on one."
  "Out-of-bounds clock rule": "When a runner goes out of bounds, the game clock normally restarts as soon as the ball is re-spotted and the referee signals ready for play; after the two-minute warning of the first half and in the last five minutes of the game it stays stopped until the next snap."
  "Four-minute offense": "The mirror image of the two-minute drill: a team protecting a lead late in the game runs the ball, keeps receivers in bounds and lets the play clock run down before every snap, so that each first down takes a minute or more off the clock."
  "Victory formation": {def: "The formation a leading team uses to end a half or game by kneeling: the quarterback under center, the line in tight, two backs just behind him to protect the ball and one deep player as a last line of defense against a fumble. The quarterback takes the snap and drops to one knee, and the clock keeps running.", aliases: ["Kneel-down"]}
  "Hail Mary": "A long, high pass thrown into a crowd of receivers and defenders near or in the end zone on the last play of a half, hoping someone on the offense catches it or a tipped ball falls to a teammate. Named after Roger Staubach's 1975 playoff touchdown."
  "Prevent defense": "A defense, used when protecting a lead in the last seconds of a half, that rushes three or four and drops seven or eight defenders deep, conceding short completions in front of it in order to take away anything long and to tackle the catch in bounds."
  "Intentional safety": "Deliberately giving the opponent two points by having the ball carrier (usually the punter) run out of the back of his own end zone, to burn clock and to replace a dangerous punt from deep in your own territory with a free kick from your own 20."
  "Fair-catch kick": "A free field-goal try, place-kicked from the spot of a fair catch with the defense ten yards away and no snap. The receiving team may choose it after any fair catch, even with time expired; a successful kick is worth three points."
  "Go-for-it decision": "The choice on fourth down between going for the first down (or touchdown), kicking a field goal and punting, increasingly made with expected-points or win-probability models rather than habit."
  "Two-point chart": "A lookup table, keyed by the score margin right after a touchdown, telling a coach whether to kick the extra point or go for two; the classic version assumes few scores remain, so it matters most late in a game."
  "Overtime rules": "The NFL's rules for a game tied after four quarters. Since 2022 in the playoffs and 2025 in the regular season, both teams get a chance to possess the ball (unless the kicking team scores a safety on the first possession) and the next score wins after that. Regular-season overtime is one 10-minute period and can end in a tie; playoff overtime continues in 15-minute periods until there is a winner."

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (helpers for this chapter's drawings)"

import logging
import os
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Rectangle, Patch, Ellipse
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, style, offense, defense, routes as r, draw_marker, animate, frame_strip
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH, MIDDLE
from gridiron.data import pbp

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
OC, DC = style.OFFENSE_DARK, style.DEFENSE_DARK
GREEN = "#0f7a55"                 # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on light fills
RUN_C, STOP_C, MAYBE_C = "#dff3ea", "#fbe3d9", "#fdf0cc"


def pct(v, d=0):
    return f"{100 * v:.{d}f}%"


def mmss(sec):
    sec = int(round(sec))
    return f"{sec // 60}:{sec % 60:02d}"


# --- boxes and arrows for flowcharts and timelines ------------------------------------------------
def blank(ax):
    ax.set_axis_off()
    ax.set_aspect("auto")


def box(ax, x, y, w, h, text, fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1.0, fs=8.0, bold=False,
        color=style.INK, sub=None, sub_fs=6.6):
    """A rounded box centred on (x, y) in data units, with an optional smaller subtitle."""
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=1.0",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=3))
    if sub:
        ax.text(x, y + h * 0.2, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal", zorder=4, linespacing=1.1)
        ax.text(x, y - h * 0.17, sub, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=sub_fs, color=style.INK_2,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.15)
    else:
        ax.text(x, y, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=color,
                fontweight="bold" if bold else "normal", zorder=4, linespacing=1.15)


def arrow(ax, p0, p1, color=style.INK_2, lw=1.1, ls="-", rad=0.0, head=9, z=2):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(p0, p1, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color, lw=lw,
                                 ls=ls, shrinkA=1, shrinkB=1, connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}", zorder=z))


# --- labels on a drawn field ---------------------------------------------------------------------
def P_(fld, p, d, w):
    """(d, w) in the offense's frame -> plot coordinates on this drawn field."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.6, ha="center", weight="normal", box_ec="none"):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = P_(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.1, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=box_ec, lw=0.6,
                                           alpha=0.92))


def lead(fld, p, frm, to, color=style.MUTED):
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = P_(fld, p, *frm), P_(fld, p, *to)
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=color, lw=0.7, zorder=7.5)


def no_numbers(fld):
    """Remove the painted yard numbers (they compete with labels on zoomed diagrams)."""
    for t in list(fld.ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit():
            t.remove()


def band(fld, x0, x1, y0, y1, color, alpha=0.12, z=0.6):
    """A shaded rectangle in BDB coordinates (x along the field, y across it)."""
    (ax_, ay_), (bx_, by_) = fld.xy(x0, y0), fld.xy(x1, y1)
    lo_x, hi_x = sorted([float(ax_), float(bx_)])
    lo_y, hi_y = sorted([float(ay_), float(by_)])
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((lo_x, lo_y), hi_x - lo_x, hi_y - lo_y, fc=color, ec="none", alpha=alpha,
                               zorder=z))


def scorebug(ax, x, y, lines, fs=7.2, ha="left"):
    """A small dark 'score bug' box with the situation, in axes-fraction coordinates."""
    ax.text(x, y, "\n".join(lines), transform=ax.transAxes, ha=ha, va="top", fontsize=fs, color="white",
            linespacing=1.35, zorder=20, family="DejaVu Sans Mono",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.45", fc="#22313f", ec="none"))


def show_play(play, times, title=None, ncols=4):
    """HTML: a scrubbable video of the simulated tracking. PDF: a one-row frame strip at `times`."""
    df = play.to_tracking(t_after=0.8)
    if PDF:
        fig = frame_strip(df, times=times, ncols=ncols, title=title, to_go=None, lateral_pad=3.0)
        for ax in fig.axes:
            for t in list(ax.texts):
                if t.get_text().isdigit():
                    t.remove()
        plt.show()
        return
    anim = animate(df, title=title)
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(anim._fig)
    display(HTML(html))
```

```{python}
COLS = ["season", "season_type", "week", "game_id", "play_id", "drive", "qtr", "time",
        "half_seconds_remaining", "game_seconds_remaining", "posteam", "defteam", "down", "ydstogo",
        "yardline_100", "play_type", "desc", "wp", "score_differential", "complete_pass",
        "incomplete_pass", "out_of_bounds", "timeout", "timeout_team", "qb_spike", "qb_kneel", "penalty",
        "pass_attempt", "air_yards", "touchdown", "interception", "fourth_down_converted",
        "two_point_attempt", "two_point_conv_result", "extra_point_result", "field_goal_result",
        "kick_distance", "posteam_timeouts_remaining", "defteam_timeouts_remaining",
        "total_home_score", "total_away_score", "safety"]
raw = pbp(range(2010, 2026), columns=COLS).sort_values(["game_id", "play_id"]).reset_index(drop=True)
reg = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"].copy()
S = {}                                   # numbers quoted in the text

# --- what each ending costs a hurrying offense (2016-2025) ----------------------------------------
h = reg[reg.season >= 2016].copy()
g = h.groupby("game_id")
for c in ["play_type", "qb_spike", "half_seconds_remaining", "drive", "timeout", "timeout_team"]:
    h["n1_" + c] = g[c].shift(-1)
    h["n2_" + c] = g[c].shift(-2)
h["gap"] = h.half_seconds_remaining - h.n1_half_seconds_remaining
late = h[h.qtr.isin([2, 4]) & h.half_seconds_remaining.between(20, 110) & (h.score_differential <= 0)
         & (h.penalty == 0) & h.play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])]
same = (late.n1_drive == late.drive) & (late.n1_timeout == 0)
inb = late[(late.complete_pass == 1) & (late.out_of_bounds == 0)]
prices = {
    "Incomplete pass": late[(late.incomplete_pass == 1) & same & (late.n1_qb_spike == 0)
                            & late.n1_play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])].gap,
    "Completion, out of bounds": late[(late.complete_pass == 1) & (late.out_of_bounds == 1) & same
                                      & late.n1_play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])].gap,
    "Completion in bounds,\nthen a timeout": inb[(inb.n1_timeout == 1) & (inb.n1_timeout_team == inb.posteam)].gap,
    "Completion in bounds,\nthen a spike": inb[same.loc[inb.index] & (inb.n1_qb_spike == 1)].gap,
    "Completion in bounds,\nthen the next real play": inb[same.loc[inb.index] & (inb.n1_qb_spike == 0)
                                                     & inb.n1_play_type.isin(["pass", "run"])].gap,
}
PRICE = {k: float(v.median()) for k, v in prices.items()}
PRICE_N = {k: int(v.size) for k, v in prices.items()}
S["p_inc"] = f"{PRICE['Incomplete pass']:.0f}"
S["p_oob"] = f"{PRICE['Completion, out of bounds']:.0f}"
S["p_to"] = f"{PRICE['Completion in bounds,' + chr(10) + 'then a timeout']:.0f}"
S["p_spike"] = f"{PRICE['Completion in bounds,' + chr(10) + 'then a spike']:.0f}"
S["p_hurry"] = f"{PRICE['Completion in bounds,' + chr(10) + 'then the next real play']:.0f}"
spk = h[(h.qb_spike == 1) & (h.n1_drive == h.drive)]
S["spike_cost"] = f"{spk.gap.median():.0f}"
S["spikes_yr"] = f"{h[h.qb_spike == 1].groupby('season').size().mean():.0f}"
kn = h[(h.qb_kneel == 1) & (h.n1_drive == h.drive) & (h.n1_timeout == 0)]
S["kneel_gap"] = f"{kn.gap.median():.0f}"
S["kneels_yr"] = f"{h[h.qb_kneel == 1].groupby('season').size().mean():.0f}"

# --- Hail Marys: deep throws from 40+ yards out with 8 or fewer seconds left in a half ------------
hm = h[(h.pass_attempt == 1) & h.qtr.isin([2, 4]) & (h.half_seconds_remaining <= 8) & (h.yardline_100 >= 40)
       & ((h.air_yards >= 35) | h.air_yards.isna())]
S["hm_n"], S["hm_td"], S["hm_int"] = f"{len(hm)}", pct(hm.touchdown.mean()), pct(hm.interception.mean())

# --- fourth downs --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
f4 = reg[(reg.down == 4) & reg.play_type.isin(["run", "pass", "punt", "field_goal"])].copy()
f4["go"] = f4.play_type.isin(["run", "pass"])

S["gon10"], S["gon17"], S["gon25"] = pct(GO.iloc[0, 1]), pct(GO.loc[2017].iloc[1]), pct(GO.iloc[-1, 1])
went = f4[f4.go & (f4.season >= 2021)].copy()

S["c1"], S["c2"], S["c3"], S["c45"] = pct(CONV[1]), pct(CONV[2]), pct(CONV[3]), pct(went[went.ydstogo.between(4, 5)].conv.mean())
S["c610"] = pct(went[went.ydstogo.between(6, 10)].conv.mean())
early3 = f4[(f4.qtr <= 3) & (f4.season >= 2022)]

        "NYJ": "Jets", "PHI": "Eagles", "PIT": "Steelers", "SEA": "Seahawks", "SF": "49ers", "TB": "Buccaneers",
        "TEN": "Titans", "WAS": "Commanders"}
S["team2"], S["team2_go"] = NICK[TEAM.index[1]], pct(TEAM.iloc[1])
yr_lead = f4[(f4.qtr <= 3) & (f4.season.between(2021, 2025))].groupby(["season", "posteam"]).go.mean()
S["det_firsts"] = ["none", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five"][int(sum(yr_lead.loc[s].idxmax() == "DET" for s in range(2021, 2026)))]

# --- field goals: make rate by distance, 2023-2025 (for the fourth-down drill) -----------------
fg = reg[(reg.play_type == "field_goal") & (reg.season >= 2023)]
S["fg5054"] = pct((fg[fg.kick_distance.between(50, 54)].field_goal_result == "made").mean())
d2 = f4[(f4.season >= 2023) & (f4.qtr <= 3) & (f4.ydstogo == 2) & f4.yardline_100.between(31, 40)]
S["go_4th2_opp"] = pct(d2.go.mean())
d2o = f4[(f4.season.between(2013, 2015)) & (f4.qtr <= 3) & (f4.ydstogo == 2) & f4.yardline_100.between(31, 40)]
S["go_4th2_old"] = pct(d2o.go.mean())

# --- tries since the 2015 extra-point change ------------------------------------------------------
tries = reg[reg.season >= 2015]
two = tries[tries.two_point_attempt == 1]
xp = tries[tries.play_type == "extra_point"]
S["two_rate"] = pct((two.two_point_conv_result == "success").mean())
S["xp_rate"] = pct((xp.extra_point_result == "good").mean(), 1)
S["two_ev"] = f"{2 * (two.two_point_conv_result == 'success').mean():.2f}"
S["xp_ev"] = f"{(xp.extra_point_result == 'good').mean():.2f}"
S["two_n15"], S["two_n25"] = f"{(two.season == 2015).sum()}", f"{(two.season == 2025).sum()}"
S["two_n14"] = f"{((reg.season == 2014) & (reg.two_point_attempt == 1)).sum()}"

# --- where the opponent starts after an end-zone punt vs after a safety kick (2015-2025) ----------
k = reg[reg.season >= 2015]
gk = k.groupby("game_id")
nxt = pd.DataFrame({"yl": gk.yardline_100.shift(-1), "pt": gk.play_type.shift(-1),
                    "yl2": gk.yardline_100.shift(-2), "pt2": gk.play_type.shift(-2)})
start = np.where(nxt.pt.isin(["run", "pass", "no_play", "qb_kneel"]), nxt.yl, nxt.yl2)
k = k.assign(next_start=start)
ez_punt = k[(k.play_type == "punt") & (k.yardline_100 >= 96)]
sk = k[(k.play_type == "kickoff") & k.desc.str.contains(r"from \w+ 20 ", regex=True, na=False)

S["ezp_n"], S["sk_n"] = f"{len(ez_punt)}", f"{len(sk)}"
S["ezp_start"] = f"{ez_punt.next_start.median():.0f}"            # the punting team's yard line
S["sk_start"] = f"{100 - sk.next_start.median():.0f}"            # the receiving team's own yard line
S["safety_gain"] = f"{sk.next_start.median() - ez_punt.next_start.median():.0f}"
```

Super Bowl LVIII, fourth quarter. San Francisco has just kicked a field goal to lead 19–16, and Kansas
City takes over at its own 25 with **1:53** on the clock and two timeouts. It sounds like plenty of
time. Is it? Seventy-five yards from a touchdown and about 40 from a long field goal, 113 seconds is less
than it looks: a completion over the middle costs about 20 of them, a sack more, an incompletion only five. Over
the next 107 seconds Kansas City will run eleven snaps, call one timeout, get two plays out of bounds
and kick a field goal with three seconds left. Then the game goes to an overtime whose
rules were rewritten after a Chiefs game two years earlier. This chapter explains every one of those
choices, and the fourth-down revolution that changed how coaches spend the other 58 minutes.

**You'll be able to:**

- Price any play in game-clock seconds, and say whether the clock will run after it, using the
  out-of-bounds clock rule and the late-game exceptions.
- Run a two-minute drill in your head: which throws save time, when to spike and when to use a
  timeout, and why a 10-second runoff can end a half.
- Do the kneel-down arithmetic for a team protecting a lead, and recognise the four-minute offense and
  the victory formation.
- Make end-of-half calls: take the points or take a shot, Hail Mary or field goal, and spot the rare
  plays that decide close games, the intentional safety and the fair-catch kick.
- Use simple fourth-down and two-point heuristics, and explain how and why the league's go-for-it rate
  rose after 2017.
- Apply the current overtime rules (playoffs since 2022, regular season since 2025) and predict how
  each team will play them.

## The clock is a currency, and the two teams want opposite things

For 56 minutes of a typical game the clock is background noise. Then, at some point in the fourth
quarter (and again at the end of the first half), it becomes the most important player on the field. The
reason is simple: possessions are scarce, and time is what possessions are made of. A team that is behind
needs **plays per second**: as many snaps as it can squeeze into the time left. A team that is ahead
wants **seconds per play**: the fewest snaps, each taking as long as possible, so the opponent gets the
ball back late or never.

Everything in this chapter follows from those two goals, and from one fact you met in the first chapter:
the clock keeps running after a ball carrier is tackled in bounds and stops after almost everything else.
So the first skill is pricing. How many seconds does each kind of play cost a team in a hurry? You can
measure it. The play-by-play data records the game clock at every snap, so the gap between two snaps is
what the first play, and whatever happened after it, cost.

```{python}
#| label: fig-clock-prices
#| fig-cap: "What a play costs a hurrying offense. Median game-clock seconds from one snap to the next, for offenses trailing or tied in the last two minutes of the first half and the last two minutes of the game (2016-2025 regular seasons, no penalties; numbers in brackets are plays). An incompletion or a catch that goes out of bounds costs only the five or six seconds the play itself takes. A catch in bounds keeps the clock running while everyone sprints back to the line: about 16 seconds if the offense then spikes the ball (which also uses up a down), about 21 if it lines up and runs a real play. A timeout stops the bleeding for the price of the timeout. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
lab = list(PRICE)
vals = [PRICE[k] for k in lab]
cols = [style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[0], style.SERIES[2], style.SERIES[1], style.SERIES[1]]
note = ["the clock stops at once", "the clock stops at once (late in a half)", "...and costs a timeout",
        "...and costs a down", "the dearest: no stoppage at all"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.3))
y = np.arange(len(lab))[::-1]
ax.barh(y, vals, color=cols, height=0.6, zorder=2)
for yi, v, k, n in zip(y, vals, lab, note):
    ax.text(v + 0.5, yi, f"{v:.0f} s", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
    ax.text(v + 3.6, yi, f"[{PRICE_N[k]:,}]  {n}", va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_yticks(y, lab, fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 52)
ax.set_xticks([0, 10, 20, 30])
ax.set_xlabel("Game-clock seconds from this snap to the next (median)")
ax.set_title("Late in a half, every way a play can end has a price")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

Read it as a price list. The cheapest plays are the ones that stop the clock by themselves: an incomplete
pass, or a completion where the receiver gets out of bounds. Each costs only the five or six seconds the
play takes. The expensive one is the catch in bounds, because the clock keeps running while eleven
players run back to the line, the officials spot the ball and the quarterback relays the next call. That
costs about `{python} S["p_hurry"]` seconds if the offense simply runs its next play. Offenses have two
ways to cut the bill. A **timeout** brings the cost back down to the play itself
(`{python} S["p_to"]` seconds) but spends one of only three. A spike, which you'll meet properly
below, stops the clock about `{python} S["p_spike"]` seconds after the previous snap, and spends a down
instead.

That is why two-minute offenses throw toward the sideline, why defenses protecting a lead try to tackle
receivers *inside* the field, and why coaches hoard timeouts like cash. A team with 1:53 and two timeouts
can afford roughly five or six in-bounds completions and a few incompletions. That is enough for 50 or 60
yards. It is not as much as it sounds.

### The out-of-bounds clock rule

One line in the price list has a condition attached. "Out of bounds stops the clock" is true only late in
a half. The full rule, which this course calls the
[**out-of-bounds clock rule**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-out-of-bounds-clock-rule), is this:
when a runner goes out of bounds, the officials stop the clock, put the ball back on the hash, and
**restart the clock when the referee signals the ball ready for play**, well before the next snap. The
exceptions are the moments when time matters most. After the **two-minute warning of the first half**,
and inside the **last five minutes of the game**, the clock stays stopped **until the snap**. (So does the
first snap after a change of possession, at any time.)[^oobrule]

```{python}
#| label: fig-oob-window
#| fig-cap: "When does getting out of bounds actually save time? The game's 60 minutes, quarter by quarter. In the white stretches (most of the game), a runner who goes out of bounds stops the clock only for the few seconds it takes to re-spot the ball; it restarts on the referee's ready signal. In the shaded windows (after the two-minute warning of the first half, and the last five minutes of the fourth quarter) it stays stopped until the next snap. The rule's asymmetry is deliberate: the fourth-quarter window is wider because the end of a game decides the result."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.1))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(-1, 61)
ax.set_ylim(-3.2, 5.2)
for q in range(4):
    x0 = q * 15
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, 0), 15, 2, fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1))
    ax.text(x0 + 7.5, 1.0, f"Q{q + 1}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK_2, zorder=4)
for x0, w, txt in [(28, 2, "last 2:00\nof the half"), (55, 5, "last 5:00\nof the game")]:
    ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, 0), w, 2, fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.2, zorder=2))
    ax.text(x0 + w / 2, 2.4, txt, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color=DC, fontweight="bold",
            linespacing=1.1)
ax.plot([30, 30], [-0.4, 2.6], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.4, zorder=3)
ax.text(30, 4.9, "halftime", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(14, -0.9, "out of bounds: clock restarts on the ready signal (seconds later)", ha="center",
        va="top", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.text(45, -0.9, "inside the shaded windows: clock\nstopped until the snap", ha="center", va="top",
        fontsize=7, color=DC, linespacing=1.1)
plt.show()
```

Why the exception? Because without it the end of every close game would be a parade of five-yard sideline
throws, each stopping the clock for free. Early in the game the league *wants* the clock to keep moving
(television windows are three hours), so out of bounds costs the offense only a few seconds of saving.
Late in a half the rule hands the trailing team a lifeline: it can save time without spending timeouts,
as long as it can get the ball to the sideline. One detail closes a loophole: a **fumble** that goes out of
bounds restarts the clock on the ready signal at any time of the game, so nobody can fumble out of bounds
on purpose to stop it.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"He stepped out of bounds, smart: that stopped the clock." In the third quarter, or with 7:00 left in the
fourth, it barely did: the clock started again as soon as the ball was spotted, usually 25 or more seconds
before the next snap. A runner who fights for two extra yards in bounds early in the fourth quarter is
not costing his team time. The same play at 4:30 is a different story.
:::

## The two-minute drill

The [**two-minute drill**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-minute-drill) is the
[hurry-up offense](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hurry-up-offense) with a deadline: a team that needs
points before a half ends, usually with the clock already inside the two-minute warning. Teams practise it
every week as its own script, because almost every rule of normal play-calling
changes:

- **No huddle, two plays at a time.** The quarterback gets two calls through his helmet radio (or carries
  them on his wristband), so after the first one the offense can line up and snap the second without
  waiting for a signal. Many teams use one-word "clock" calls for plays the whole offense knows.
- **Throw outside.** Routes break toward the sideline (outs, comebacks, corner routes) so that the catch
  ends out of bounds. Receivers are coached to secure the ball, take one more step, and get out: never
  turn upfield for two extra yards and get tackled in bounds.
- **Middle of the field only with a plan.** A catch over the middle is worth taking if it gains a lot or
  if the offense has a timeout to spend. Otherwise it costs about 20 seconds.
- **No sacks.** A sack loses yards *and* keeps the clock running. Quarterbacks throw the ball away
  instead (out of bounds, past the line of scrimmage, or near a receiver) and accept the lost down.
- **Know the finish line.** The real target is usually not the end zone but **field-goal range**: the yard
  line from which the kicker has a good chance, with enough time left to get the field-goal unit on.

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-minute-menu
#| fig-cap: "The two-minute menu. The offense (blue) has the ball near midfield and needs about 25 yards to reach field-goal range; the defense (orange) sits back in a soft two-deep zone and invites throws underneath. The outside receivers run sideline routes: X an out at 12 yards, Z a comeback at 15 (straight up the field, then back toward the sideline). Inside, H runs a corner route toward the sideline as well and Y a seam up the middle; the back (R) checks into the flat. The shaded lanes between the numbers and the sideline are where a catch can end out of bounds and stop the clock. A completion in the middle costs about 20 seconds unless the offense calls a timeout."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
dfn = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("DLE", "DE", 1.0, -4.5), ("DLT", "DT", 1.0, -1.2), ("DRT", "DT", 1.0, 1.8), ("DRE", "DE", 1.0, 4.8),
    ("MIKE", "MIKE", 7.0, 0.5), ("LCB", "CB", 8.0, -17.2), ("RCB", "CB", 8.0, 17.2),
    ("NB", "NB", 8.0, -8.0), ("DB", "DB", 8.0, 8.5), ("FS", "FS", 17.0, -10.0), ("SS", "SS", 17.0, 10.0)]]
p2m = Play(off, dfn, los=50, to_go=10)
p2m.dropback(2.0)
p2m.route("X", r.out(12, 6))
p2m.route("Z", r.comeback(15))
p2m.route("H", r.corner(11))
p2m.route("Y", r.seam(19))
p2m.route("RB", r.flat(1.0, 6.0), side=-1)
p2m.highlight("X", "Z")
fld = p2m.draw(window=(-8, 25), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
nl, nr = p2m.ball_y + 14.6, p2m.ball_y - 14.6           # the tops of the numbers, roughly
band(fld, p2m.los - 8, p2m.los + 25, nl, FIELD_WIDTH, style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.10)
band(fld, p2m.los - 8, p2m.los + 25, 0, nr, style.SERIES[0], alpha=0.10)
say(fld, p2m, 17.5, -21.8, "catch, step\nout: clock\nstops", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p2m, 17.5, 21.8, "catch, step\nout: clock\nstops", color=OC, fs=6.4)
say(fld, p2m, 22.0, 3.0, "catch in here and get tackled:\nthe clock runs (about 20 s)\nunless you call a timeout",
    color=style.INK, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p2m, 13.5, -1.5, "soft zones: the defense\ngives the short stuff", color=DC, fs=6.3)
plt.show()
```

What does the defense do about it? It plays the same game backwards: it sits deep enough that nothing
gets behind it, keeps its cornerbacks outside the receivers so the sideline routes are contested, and
tackles in bounds. That tug-of-war, offense pulling the ball outside and defense pushing it inside, is the
whole two-minute drill in one sentence.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The two-minute drill exists because the clock rules are asymmetric. The offense can stop the clock
(incompletions, out of bounds, timeouts, spikes); the defense can only stop it with timeouts and by
forcing incompletions. So the trailing offense, uniquely, gets to *control the pace* of the end of a half.
The drill is the set of habits that turns that control into points, and it has to be rehearsed because
the habits contradict normal football: throw away from the open middle, give up yards for seconds, and
never take a sack.
:::

The drill has a long history in big games. In the 1958 NFL Championship Game, Johnny Unitas drove the
Baltimore Colts into position for Steve Myhra's tying field goal with seven seconds left, and the Colts
won in the first sudden-death overtime in NFL history.[^unitas] In January 1987 John Elway's Broncos went
98 yards in Cleveland, starting with 5:32 left ("The Drive"), to force overtime in the AFC Championship
Game. And in Super Bowl XXXVI, with the score tied, 1:21 left and no timeouts, Tom Brady took the
Patriots from their own 17 to the Rams' 30 with two spikes along the way, and Adam Vinatieri kicked the
48-yard winner as time ran out.[^xxxvi]

### The spike

A [**spike**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spike) is the quarterback taking the snap and immediately
throwing the ball into the ground. It is an incomplete pass, so the clock stops. Why isn't it
[intentional grounding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding), which is exactly
"throwing the ball away to avoid a loss with no receiver nearby"? Because the rulebook carves out an
exception for it: a quarterback under center may stop the clock legally if, *immediately* upon receiving
the snap, he begins a continuous throwing motion and throws the ball directly into the ground. If he
waits, he may not: a delayed spike is grounding.[^spikerule]

The spike costs about `{python} S["spike_cost"]` second of clock and **a down**. That second cost is the
real one. Spiking on first down is cheap (second-and-10 is fine in a two-minute drill); spiking on second
down leaves only one real play before fourth down; spiking on third down is almost always a mistake.
Teams spike about `{python} S["spikes_yr"]` times a season in all. You will see it most often in the
sequence the price list describes: an in-bounds completion, a frantic sprint to the line, the line set,
and the ball slammed into the turf with 15 to 20 seconds gone.

When should a team with a timeout spike instead of using the timeout? When there is time for more plays
after it. A timeout is the more valuable token, because it keeps the down. Coaches spend timeouts late,
for the field goal (the kicking unit needs a stopped clock to run onto the field) or for a catch in the
middle near the end, and use the spike to keep them.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper: the fake spike"}
Once everyone expects a spike, the threat of one is a weapon. On November 27, 1994, against the Jets,
Dan Marino ran to the line at the Jets' 8 with under 40 seconds left, shouted "Clock! Clock!", made the spike motion, and
instead threw a touchdown to Mark Ingram while the defense straightened up; the Dolphins won 28–24.[^marino]
The fake spike still shows up occasionally, and it is why a defense facing a hurried line-up can never
completely relax. It works only because the real spike is so common.
:::

### Timeouts and the 10-second runoff

Timeouts are the scarcest resource in the two minutes: three per half, and none carry over. Their value
depends on when they are used. A timeout early in a half saves the 20-odd seconds between plays, but those
seconds rarely matter. The same timeout in the last minute can be the difference between a field goal
and no field goal. That's why you'll hear announcers criticise a coach for "wasting" a timeout on a
substitution mix-up in the third quarter: it is the end-of-half timeout he's spending.

The rules guard the clock against cheap tricks. After the two-minute warning of either half, if the
offense stops the clock by breaking a rule (a false start or other foul while the clock is running,
intentional grounding, an illegal forward pass, a backward pass thrown out of bounds, spiking the ball
*after* a play has ended), the officials take **ten seconds off the game clock**, the
[**10-second runoff**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-10-second-runoff), and restart it on the ready
signal. The offense may spend a timeout instead, if it has one, and the defense may decline the runoff
along with the yardage penalty. A defense is never charged a runoff: if it fouls to stop the clock, the
clock simply starts on the ready signal, and in the last 40 seconds a defensive time-saving foul can
end the half if the defense has no timeouts left.[^runoff]

The runoff also applies when a **replay** changes a stopped clock into a running one after the two-minute
warning. If a receiver ruled out of bounds is shown to have been tackled in bounds, the clock should never
have stopped, so ten seconds come off, and neither team can decline them (either can use a timeout to
prevent them). **Either half can end on a runoff**, and one famous game did.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Falcons at Lions, 2017 — ended by a runoff"}
Week 3 of the 2017 season, Atlanta led Detroit 30–26 in the last seconds. Detroit had no timeouts. On
third-and-goal from the 1 with 12 seconds left, Matthew Stafford hit Golden Tate on a short pass, and the
officials signalled touchdown. The booth reviewed it (all scoring plays are reviewed), and the replay
showed Tate down short of the goal line, at the 1. A touchdown stops the clock; a runner tackled in bounds
does not. The clock had stopped with eight seconds left; under the replay rule it goes back to the moment
the play should have ended and then runs ten seconds, and with fewer than ten seconds left the game is
simply over.[^falcons] What to notice: the Lions lost not because the play
failed by a foot, but because they had no timeout to absorb the runoff. A single timeout saved for the
end would have bought one more snap from the 1.
:::

### An annotated two-minute drive

Back to the opening scene. Here is every snap of Kansas City's drive at the end of regulation in Super
Bowl LVIII, plotted the way a clock manager thinks about it: time on one axis, field position on the
other.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lviii-drive
#| fig-cap: "Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024), Kansas City's drive at the end of regulation, trailing 19-16. Each dot is a snap, placed at its game clock and the ball's spot; the line to the next dot is green when the clock kept running between the snaps and orange when it was stopped. Kansas City used the cheap stoppages (three incompletions, a scramble and a catch that went out of bounds), spent only one of its two timeouts, after a first down near midfield, and kicked the tying field goal with three seconds left, still holding a timeout in case it needed one for the kick. Source: nflverse play-by-play, game 2023_22_SF_KC."
lv = raw[(raw.game_id == "2023_22_SF_KC") & (raw.qtr == 4) & (raw.half_seconds_remaining <= 113)].copy()
snaps = lv[(lv.posteam == "KC") & lv.play_type.isin(["pass", "run", "field_goal"])].copy()
snaps["t"] = snaps.half_seconds_remaining
snaps["own"] = 100 - snaps.yardline_100                      # yards from KC's own goal line
KEY = {3769: "1st & 10 KC 25: Kelce 9, in bounds",
       3794: "2nd & 1: Mahomes scramble 3, out of bounds",
       3816: "1st & 10: Gray 12, in bounds",
       3841: "1st & 10: Watson 8, in bounds",
       3866: "2nd & 2: incomplete",
       3889: "3rd & 2: McKinnon 7, first down;\n    KC timeout at 0:40",
       3914: "1st & 10 SF 36: Mahomes scramble 3,\n    in bounds (timeout kept)",
       3943: "2nd & 7: incomplete",
       3966: "3rd & 7: Kelce 22, pushed out at\n    the SF 11; SF timeout at 0:10",
       3994: "1st & 10: incomplete",
       4027: "2nd & 10: Butker 29-yd field goal,\n    19-19 with 0:03 left"}
running = {3769: True, 3794: False, 3816: True, 3841: True, 3866: False, 3889: True, 3914: True,
           3943: False, 3966: False, 3994: False}
NUDGE = {3866: (0, -4.5), 3889: (0, 4.5), 3943: (0, 4.5), 3966: (0, -4.5), 3994: (0, -4.5), 4027: (0, 4.5)}
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 3.9))
ax = fig.add_axes([0.09, 0.13, 0.52, 0.78])
kx = fig.add_axes([0.63, 0.05, 0.37, 0.88])
blank(kx)
pts = snaps[["play_id", "t", "own"]].values
for (pid, t0, y0), (_, t1, y1) in zip(pts[:-1], pts[1:]):
    c = GREEN if running[int(pid)] else style.DEFENSE
    ax.plot([t0, t1], [y0, y1], color=c, lw=2.2, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="round")
for i, (pid, t, y) in enumerate(pts, start=1):
    dx, dy = NUDGE.get(int(pid), (0, 0))
    ax.scatter([t + dx], [y + dy], s=105, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, zorder=4, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.8)
    if dy:
        ax.plot([t, t + dx], [y, y + dy * 0.6], color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, lw=0.7, zorder=3)
    ax.text(t + dx, y + dy, str(i), ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3, color="white", fontweight="bold", zorder=5)
for t, txt in [(40, "KC timeout"), (10, "SF timeout")]:
    ax.axvline(t, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
    ax.text(t - 1.2, 18, txt, fontsize=6.2, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom", rotation=90)
ax.axhline(65, color=style.LINE_TO_GAIN, lw=1.2, zorder=1)
ax.text(114, 66.5, "long field-goal range begins\n(about the SF 35)", fontsize=6.2, color="#9a6a00", ha="left",
        va="bottom", linespacing=1.05)
ax.set_xlim(116, -2)
ax.set_ylim(15, 98)
ax.set_xticks([113, 90, 60, 30, 0], ["1:53", "1:30", "1:00", "0:30", "0:00"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_yticks([25, 40, 50, 60, 75, 89], ["KC 25", "KC 40", "50", "SF 40", "SF 25", "SF 11"], fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Game clock", fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Ball on", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Kansas City's last drive of regulation", fontsize=9.5)
ax.legend(handles=[Line2D([], [], color=GREEN, lw=2.2, label="clock ran to next snap"),
                   Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=2.2, label="clock stopped")],
          loc="upper left", fontsize=6.5)
for i, pid in enumerate(KEY, start=1):
    yy = 0.97 - (i - 1) * 0.088
    kx.scatter([0.03], [yy], s=80, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, transform=kx.transAxes, clip_on=False)
    kx.text(0.03, yy, str(i), transform=kx.transAxes, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6, color="white",
            fontweight="bold")
    kx.text(0.09, yy, KEY[pid], transform=kx.transAxes, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK,
            linespacing=1.05)
```
