
Four things are worth noticing, because they are what good clock management looks like.

1. **The cheap plays came early.** The first snap was a 9-yard catch in bounds, and then Mahomes, facing
   second-and-1, scrambled and **got out of bounds**. Inside the last five minutes, that stopped the clock
   until the next snap. The drive used about 40 seconds to reach midfield, and Kansas City still had both
   timeouts.
2. **One timeout, when the price was high.** After a third-down conversion at the 49ers' 36 with the
   clock running, the Chiefs called their timeout at 0:40, saving about 20 seconds at the moment the
   seconds started to matter.
3. **A timeout in the pocket.** After Mahomes's scramble to the 33 stayed in bounds, Kansas City
   *didn't* use its last timeout; it hurried to the line and threw incomplete at 0:21. The timeout was
   insurance: as long as the Chiefs held it, any catch, anywhere, could be followed by a field goal.
4. **The decisive catch went out of bounds.** On third-and-7 with 16 seconds left, Travis Kelce caught a pass and was
   pushed out at the 11, stopping the clock at 0:10. One more shot at the end zone, an incompletion, and Harrison Butker
   tied the game with three seconds left.[^lviii]

Notice also what San Francisco did *before* the drive. On fourth-and-5 at the Chiefs' 35, with 1:57 left
and the score tied, the 49ers kicked a 53-yard field goal to lead by three. A touchdown there would have
forced Kansas City to score a touchdown; the field goal let it tie with a field goal. That is the
end-of-half trade-off this chapter returns to later.

## The four-minute offense: when the clock is on your side

Flip the situation. You lead by six with four minutes left and you have the ball. Now every second the
clock runs is a second the other team can't use. The
[**four-minute offense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-minute-offense) is the two-minute drill
in reverse:

- **Run the ball, and run it inside**, where the ball carrier will be tackled in bounds. A 3-yard run that
  keeps the clock moving beats a 12-yard pass that might fall incomplete.
- **Use the whole play clock.** Snap with one or two seconds left on the 40-second clock. A first down
  then costs the opponent about 40 seconds per play, or about two minutes per set of downs, if it has no
  timeouts.
- **Ball security over yards.** A fumble or an interception hands the opponent both the ball and the clock.
- **First downs end games.** The point of the drive is not points; it is a fresh set of downs, each worth
  roughly two more minutes. Teams sometimes stay in bounds or even go down short of the goal line, rather
  than score and give the ball back.

The defense's counter is timeouts, used immediately after each running play stays in bounds, and
everything it can do to force an incompletion or a punt. A defense with three timeouts and the two-minute
warning to come can stop the clock four times; with none, it can only hope for a stop.

### The kneel-down arithmetic

At some point the leading team doesn't need any more yards. It only needs the clock to run out, and the
safest play in football is the quarterback kneeling down. Each kneel uses a down and takes about two
seconds, and the clock keeps running afterwards, because the quarterback is "tackled" in bounds. Between
kneels the offense lets the 40-second play clock run almost to zero. In the play-by-play, consecutive
kneels with no timeout between them come about `{python} S["kneel_gap"]` seconds apart.

So the question every leading team asks when it gets a first down late in the game is: **can we kneel it
out from here?** With three downs to use (a fourth-down kneel would hand the ball over if time remained),
it's arithmetic.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kneel-math
#| fig-cap: "The kneel-down arithmetic. The leading team has first-and-10 and the clock is running, with a fresh 40-second play clock. Each kneel lets the play clock run down (green, about 39 seconds) and then takes about two seconds (dark blue). Every timeout the defense has left stops the clock after a kneel, and the next snap then starts the clock again at once (orange tick), so that play clock costs nothing. With no timeouts, three kneels drain about 2:03; each timeout takes about 40 seconds off that. The two-minute warning works exactly like one more defensive timeout if the kneels cross it. With three timeouts, the third one leaves the offense facing fourth down with time still on the clock."
PLAYCLK, KNEEL = 39, 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 2.7))
rows = []
for n_to in range(4):
    segs, t, used = [], 0, 0
    clock_running = True
    for kneel in range(3):
        if clock_running:
            segs.append((t, PLAYCLK, "pc"))
            t += PLAYCLK
        segs.append((t, KNEEL, "kn"))
        t += KNEEL
        if used < n_to:
            used += 1
            segs.append((t, 0, "to"))
            clock_running = False
        else:
            clock_running = True
    rows.append((n_to, segs, t))
for n_to, segs, total in rows:
    yy = 3 - n_to
    for x0, w, kind in segs:
        if kind == "pc":
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yy - 0.28), w, 0.56, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, lw=0.8))
        elif kind == "kn":
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, yy - 0.28), w, 0.56, fc=style.OFFENSE_DARK, ec="none"))
        else:
            ax.plot([x0 + 0.6, x0 + 0.6], [yy - 0.42, yy + 0.42], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2)
    ax.text(total + 2.5, yy, f"{mmss(total)} drained", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_yticks([3, 2, 1, 0], ["0 timeouts", "1 timeout", "2 timeouts", "3 timeouts"], fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Defense has")
ax.set_xlim(0, 150)
ax.set_ylim(-0.7, 3.7)
ax.set_xticks([0, 30, 60, 90, 120], ["0:00", "0:30", "1:00", "1:30", "2:00"])
ax.set_xlabel("Game clock drained by three kneels (from a fresh play clock with the clock running)")
ax.set_title("How much clock three kneel-downs can kill")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(handles=[Patch(fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, label="play clock runs (≈39 s)"),
                   Patch(fc=style.OFFENSE_DARK, label="kneel (≈2 s)"),
                   Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=2.2, label="defense timeout")],
          loc="lower right", fontsize=7, ncol=1)
plt.show()
```

The rule of thumb that falls out: **with no defensive timeouts, a first down with about two minutes or less
on a running clock ends the game.** Each timeout the defense holds is worth about 40 seconds, which is why
a defense down by four with 2:30 left will start calling timeouts after the *first* running play, not wait.
And it is why a timeout is worth more to the team *without* the ball late in the game: it is the only
thing that converts the offense's play clock back into usable time.

Two famous games show the leading team taking this arithmetic to its logical end. In December 2007, the
Eagles led Dallas 10–6 when Brian Westbrook broke a run into the clear with Dallas out of timeouts; he
deliberately went down at the 1 instead of scoring, and Donovan McNabb knelt three times to end the
game.[^westbrook] A touchdown would have given Dallas the ball back with about two minutes left; the
kneels gave it nothing. And in Super Bowl XLVI, the Patriots, leading by two, *let* Ahmad Bradshaw score
with 57 seconds left (he tried to stop at the 1 and fell into the end zone), so that Tom Brady would get
the ball back with time on the clock rather than watch the Giants run it down for a chip-shot field
goal.[^xlvi] Both are the four-minute offense seen from either side: the team with the ball values the clock
more than six points, and the defense will pay six points for the clock.

### The victory formation

The kneel is so routine that it has its own formation, the
[**victory formation**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-victory-formation), and announcers call the
play a [**kneel-down**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-kneel-down).

```{python}
#| label: fig-victory
#| fig-cap: "The victory formation. Seven blockers on the line in tight splits (no gaps for a defender to shoot), both tight ends attached. The quarterback (Q) is under center; two backs stand just behind him on either side, close enough to block a defender who slips through and to fall on the ball if the snap is fumbled. One deep player (S, often a safety or a receiver) stands 12 or more yards back as a last line of defense: if the ball somehow comes loose and a defender scoops it up, he is the only one who can stop a touchdown return. The quarterback takes the snap and kneels; the defense usually doesn't rush hard, by an unwritten rule."
vf = [Player(k, pos, "off", d, w, label=lab) for k, pos, d, w, lab in [
    ("LT", "LT", -0.7, -3.2, ""), ("LG", "LG", -0.7, -1.6, ""), ("C", "C", -0.7, 0.0, "C"),
    ("RG", "RG", -0.7, 1.6, ""), ("RT", "RT", -0.7, 3.2, ""), ("U", "TE", -0.7, -4.8, "U"),
    ("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), ("QB", "QB", -2.2, 0.0, "Q"), ("LB_", "RB", -3.6, -1.9, "R"),
    ("RB_", "FB", -3.6, 1.9, "F"), ("DEEP", "S", -13.0, 0.0, "S")]]
vd = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -5.2), ("T1", "DT", 1.0, -1.6), ("T2", "DT", 1.0, 1.6), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 5.2),
    ("M", "MIKE", 4.5, 0.0), ("S_", "SAM", 4.5, 4.5), ("W", "WILL", 4.5, -4.5),
    ("C1", "CB", 6.0, -10.0), ("C2", "CB", 6.0, 10.0), ("FS", "FS", 10.0, -5.0), ("SS", "SS", 10.0, 5.0)]]
pv = Play(vf, vd, los=70, to_go=None)
pv.highlight("QB")
fld = pv.draw(window=(-16.5, 12.5), lateral=(-15.5, 15.5), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
say(fld, pv, -3.0, -9.6, "quarterback: snap,\ndrop to one knee", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-2.6, -6.6), (-2.2, -0.9))
say(fld, pv, -6.6, 6.9, "two backs: protect\nthe ball, block leaks", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-5.8, 4.0), (-4.3, 2.6))
say(fld, pv, -13.0, 7.6, "deep back: stops a\nfumble return", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-13.0, 4.4), (-13.0, 0.9))
say(fld, pv, -2.4, 10.0, "tight splits, both\nends attached", color=OC, fs=6.6)
lead(fld, pv, (-1.6, 7.6), (-0.9, 5.6))
plt.show()
```

The formation's history is a cautionary tale. On November 19, 1978, the Giants led the Eagles 17–12 with
about 30 seconds left and the ball. Instead of kneeling, they handed off; quarterback Joe Pisarcik and
fullback Larry Csonka botched the exchange, Eagles cornerback Herman Edwards picked up the loose ball
and ran it in, and Philadelphia won 19–17. The "Miracle at the Meadowlands" cost the Giants' offensive
coordinator his job the next day, and teams across the league began kneeling, in a formation built to
make that fumble impossible.[^meadowlands]

By convention the defense doesn't fight a kneel-down. When the Buccaneers' Greg Schiano had his defense
charge into the Giants' victory formation in September 2012, knocking Eli Manning to the ground, Tom
Coughlin confronted him at midfield and the incident became a league-wide argument about sportsmanship.
Schiano's defence was that the game wasn't over until the clock hit zero, which is true; the convention
survives because a fumble on a kneel is so unlikely that rushing it mostly risks injuries.[^schiano]

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In Madden, "kneel" is a button you press once the clock math works. In a real game somebody has to *do*
the math, under noise, with the play clock running: down, distance, the opponent's timeouts, whether the
two-minute warning is still to come. NFL staffs keep a clock-management card for exactly this (often a
dedicated assistant or the "game management" coach in the booth), and head coaches have been fired over
getting it wrong. When a broadcast shows a coach on the headset at 2:15 with the offense jogging to the
line, he is usually being read that card.
:::

## End of the half: points versus risk

The last minute of the first half has its own logic. There is no next possession to protect against
(the second half starts with a kickoff and fresh timeouts), so a team with the ball and time faces a
narrower question: **is a shot at points worth the risk of giving the opponent the ball with time to
use it?**

Three questions settle most of these calls:

1. **How far to field-goal range, and how many plays do I have?** From the price list: with one timeout,
   45 seconds is about four or five plays if half of them go out of bounds or fall incomplete. If those
   plays can plausibly gain 30 yards, go.
2. **What happens if it goes wrong?** An interception or a three-and-out deep in your own territory gives
   the opponent a short field. Backed up at your own 10 with 40 seconds, most coaches kneel.
3. **Who gets the ball to start the second half?** If you will receive the second-half kickoff, scoring
   at the end of the half is a *double score* opportunity: points just before the break, then the ball
   again immediately. That's a big reason most coaches defer when they win the coin toss.

The most famous end-of-half argument came at the end of a *game*. In Super Bowl XXXVI, with the score tied
and the Patriots starting at their own 17 with 1:21 and no timeouts, the broadcast's John Madden said they
should run out the clock: "You have to play for overtime now." Bill Belichick and Tom Brady went for it anyway, and New England won on the final
play.[^xxxvi-madden] Madden was not wrong about the risk; he was underrating the price list. Two short
throws to the running back, a spike, a third throw to the back that was pushed out of bounds, an
incompletion and Troy Brown's 23-yard catch that went out of bounds had the ball at the Rams' 36 with 21
seconds still left.

### The Hail Mary

When there is time for only one snap and the end zone is out of field-goal range, there is one play left:
the [**Hail Mary**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hail-mary). Four or five receivers sprint to one spot
in or near the end zone, the quarterback buys time and throws as high and as far as he can, and everyone
converges on the ball. The name comes from the Cowboys' 1975 playoff game at Minnesota, when Roger Staubach
threw a 50-yard winner to Drew Pearson and told reporters afterward that he had closed his eyes and said
a Hail Mary.[^staubach]

```{python}
#| label: fig-hail-mary
#| fig-cap: "A Hail Mary from the opponent's 48 with four seconds left (simulated tracking, BDB format). The five receivers (blue) race to one spot about two yards deep in the end zone; the defense (orange) rushes three and drops eight, with its deep players already near the goal line before the snap. The quarterback buys time with a deep drop and throws at about three seconds; the ball is in the air for about three more. In print, the left panel shows everyone's path from the snap and the right panels close in on the landing spot as the ball comes down and arrives (faint tails show the last second of movement). The receivers' plan is less 'catch it' than 'touch it': one man (Y) goes up for it, and the others position themselves in front of and behind him for a tip."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
off = [pl.moved(w=-17.0) if pl.key == "X" else pl.moved(w=17.0) if pl.key == "Z" else pl for pl in off]
off = [pl.moved(d=-5.0, w=1.5) if pl.key == "RB" else pl for pl in off]
hmd = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -3.5), ("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.5), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 4.0),
    ("L1", "LB", 12.0, -8.0), ("L2", "LB", 12.0, 0.0), ("L3", "LB", 12.0, 8.0),
    ("C1", "CB", 18.0, -15.0), ("C2", "CB", 18.0, 15.0),
    ("S1", "FS", 36.0, -5.0), ("S2", "SS", 36.0, 5.0), ("S3", "S", 40.0, 0.0)]]
hmp = Play(off, hmd, los=62, to_go=None)
hmp.dropback(3.0)
SPOT = 50.0                      # two yards deep in the end zone (the goal line is 48 yards away)
for key, w_end, spd in [("X", -3.0, 9.0), ("H", -1.0, 8.8), ("Y", 0.5, 8.8), ("Z", 3.0, 9.0), ("RB", 1.5, 8.6)]:
    hmp.route(key, [(SPOT - 1.5, w_end), (SPOT, w_end * 0.6)], absolute=True, speed=spd)
for key, to, delay, spd in [("S1", (SPOT - 1.0, -2.0), 0.4, 4.5), ("S2", (SPOT - 1.0, 2.0), 0.4, 4.5),
                            ("S3", (SPOT + 1.5, 0.0), 0.6, 4.5), ("C1", (SPOT - 3.5, -4.5), 0.0, 6.5),
                            ("C2", (SPOT - 3.5, 4.5), 0.0, 6.5), ("L1", (SPOT - 7.0, -3.0), 0.2, 6.2),
                            ("L2", (SPOT - 8.0, 0.0), 0.2, 6.2), ("L3", (SPOT - 7.0, 3.0), 0.2, 6.2)]:
    hmp.drop(key, to, delay=delay, speed=spd)
for key in ("E1", "N", "E2"):
    hmp.rush(key, speed=3.6)
hmp.pass_to("Y", t=3.0)
if PDF:
    # print: the whole play at the snap (left), then two close-ups of the landing spot (right)
    from gridiron import draw_frame
    trk = hmp.to_tracking(t_after=0.8)
    trk["_id"] = trk.displayName
    tmap = trk.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.6, 5.3))
    axL = fig.add_axes([0.0, 0.0, 0.45, 0.93])
    no_numbers(hmp.draw(ax=axL, window=(-10, 58), lateral=(-19.5, 19.5), title=False))
    axL.set_title("The plan, at the snap", fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    for t, (x0, y0), ttl in [(5.3, (0.47, 0.5), "+5.3 s: the crowd gathers, ball on its way"),
                             (6.3, (0.47, 0.0), "+6.3 s: the ball arrives")]:
        axr = fig.add_axes([x0, y0, 0.53, 0.43])
        fr = Field(ax=axr, orient="vertical", los=hmp.los, window=(36, 58), lateral=(hmp.ball_y - 12, hmp.ball_y + 12))
        no_numbers(fr)
        fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
        near = trk[trk.x >= hmp.los + 37.0]                       # only what is inside the close-up
        draw_frame(fr, near[near.frameId == fid], near[(near.frameId <= fid) & (near.frameId >= fid - 12)],
                   fr.pts_per_yard())
        axr.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    plt.show()
else:
    show_play(hmp, times=[0.0, 2.4, 4.4, 6.2])
```

How often does it work? Over the last ten regular seasons, throws of 35-plus air yards from 40 or more yards
out in the last eight seconds of a half, the play-by-play's best proxy for a Hail Mary, numbered
`{python} S["hm_n"]`. They produced a touchdown `{python} S["hm_td"]` of the time and an interception
`{python} S["hm_int"]` of the time.[^hailmary] One in seventeen sounds hopeless, but the alternative at
0:04 is zero, and the interception on the last play costs nothing. (At the end of the *first* half it can:
a team that throws a Hail Mary from its own 40 is risking very little, but one from deep in its own territory
can be returned.)

### The prevent defense

The defense's mirror image is the [**prevent defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-prevent-defense):
rush three (sometimes four), drop eight, and play everyone deep, conceding the short completion in order
to take away the long one and tackle in bounds.

```{python}
#| label: fig-prevent
#| fig-cap: "A prevent defense against four vertical routes. Three rushers; four deep defenders (dashed zones) 20 to 25 yards off the ball, so that nothing can be thrown over them; four more underneath at about 10 yards, sitting in the throwing lanes and ready to rally to the catch and tackle it in bounds. The open space is in front of them: the back's checkdown at 4 yards (R, ringed) and anything short of the underneath layer is free. With 25 seconds left and no timeouts, a 10-yard completion there that stays in bounds is a win for the defense."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
pd_ = [Player(k, pos, "def", d, w) for k, pos, d, w in [
    ("E1", "DE", 1.0, -3.8), ("N", "NT", 1.0, 0.0), ("E2", "DE", 1.0, 3.8),
    ("U1", "LB", 9.5, -13.0), ("U2", "LB", 9.5, -4.5), ("U3", "LB", 9.5, 4.5), ("U4", "NB", 9.5, 13.0),
    ("D1", "CB", 21.0, -18.0), ("D2", "FS", 24.0, -6.0), ("D3", "SS", 24.0, 6.0), ("D4", "CB", 21.0, 18.0)]]
pp = Play(off, pd_, los=50, to_go=None)
pp.dropback(2.0)
for key in ("X", "H", "Y", "Z"):
    pp.route(key, r.go(26))
pp.route("RB", [(1.0, 7.0), (8.5, 8.5)], frame="field")
for key in ("D1", "D2", "D3", "D4"):
    pp.zone(center=(pp.players[key].d + 3.0, pp.players[key].w), size=(10.0, 11.0))
for key, dw in (("E1", -1.0), ("N", 0.0), ("E2", 1.0)):
    pp.rush(key, pts=[(-3.8, dw)])
pp.highlight("RB")
fld = pp.draw(window=(-8, 33), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
say(fld, pp, 30.0, 0.0, "nothing gets over the top", color=DC, fs=6.8)
say(fld, pp, 13.0, 0.0, "underneath layer: rally and\ntackle the catch in bounds", color=DC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, pp, 5.5, -4.6, "free: short throws\nin front of them", color=OC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, pp, -5.0, 14.0, "three rushers:\nall the time he wants", color=DC, fs=6.4)
plt.show()
```

The prevent has a bad reputation. "The only thing the prevent defense prevents is winning" is one of
football's oldest lines, and every fan has watched a team give up 60 yards in 90 seconds while playing it.
The criticism is fair when the defense goes soft *too early*. With two minutes left and timeouts in hand,
an offense can take the free 12-yard completions all the way down the field, because the prevent concedes
yards to save time and the offense has time to spare. With 15 seconds left and no timeouts, the same
coverage is exactly right: there is time for one or two plays, so the only thing that can beat you is a
long one. The prevent is a clock-dependent call, like everything else in this chapter. What it trades away
is yards; what it buys is the end of the game. The trade is good only when the clock makes yards cheap.

### Two rare plays that decide games

#### Sidebar plate: the intentional safety

An [**intentional safety**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-safety) gives the opponent two
points on purpose. It sounds absurd until you see the situation it's for: you lead late, you're about to
punt from your own end zone, and the punt is the most dangerous play you could run. The punter is standing
almost on the end line, rushers have the shortest possible path to him, and a block or a long return can
lose the game. So instead the punter takes the snap, runs around his own end zone burning seconds (his
blockers may hold on purpose: a hold in your own end zone costs only the safety you are already taking),
and steps out of the back of it. The opponent gets two points; you then kick off from your own 20.

```{python}
#| label: fig-safety-plate
#| fig-cap: "The intentional safety, as a trade. Top: punting from your own end zone (ball at the 2). The punter stands at the end line, the rush has its shortest path to him, and after the kick and return the opponent's drive starts, at the median of 2015-2025 punts from inside the 5, near midfield in the punting team's territory (marked; course calculation). Bottom: taking the safety instead. The punter runs out of the end zone (two points to the opponent, and several seconds off the clock); then the safety kick, from your own 20 with the 2026 kickoff alignment, has to reach the landing zone (the opponent's 20 to its goal line) and is returned to about the receiving team's own 35 (median, marked). The safety buys about 20 yards of field position and removes the block-and-return risk, for two points."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 4.9))
LAT = (8.0, 45.3)
yb = MIDDLE
# top: the punt from the end zone
fa = Field(ax=axes[0], orient="horizontal", los=12, window=(-12, 108), to_go=None, lateral=LAT)
no_numbers(fa)
axa = fa.ax
ezs = int(S["ezp_start"]) + 10                                 # BDB x of the median start
draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(12, yb)), "off", "C", fa.pts_per_yard())
draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(1.8, yb)), "off", "P", fa.pts_per_yard())
for dy in (-6, -3, 3, 6):
    draw_marker(axa, *map(float, fa.xy(13.0, yb + dy)), "def", "", fa.pts_per_yard())
axa.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fa.xy(1.8, yb), fa.xy(ezs + 9, yb - 3), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                              color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.15", zorder=6))
axa.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fa.xy(ezs + 9, yb - 3), fa.xy(ezs, yb - 3), arrowstyle="-|>",
                              mutation_scale=10, color=DC, lw=2.2, zorder=6))
axa.text(*fa.xy(3, yb + 13.5), "punter at the end line:\nthe rush is 11 yards away", fontsize=6.6, ha="left",
         va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axa.text(*fa.xy(ezs + 4, yb + 9.0), f"opponent's drive starts\naround your {S['ezp_start']} (median)", fontsize=6.6,
         ha="center", va="center", color=DC, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axa.set_title("A. Punt from your own end zone", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
# bottom: the safety and the safety kick
fb = Field(ax=axes[1], orient="horizontal", los=30, window=(-30, 90), to_go=None, lateral=LAT)
no_numbers(fb)
axb = fb.ax
draw_marker(axb, *map(float, fb.xy(8.0, yb)), "off", "P", fb.pts_per_yard())
axb.plot(*zip(*[tuple(map(float, fb.xy(x, y))) for x, y in [(8.0, yb), (6.0, yb - 4), (4.0, yb - 2), (3.0, yb - 6)]]),
         color=OC, lw=1.3, zorder=6)
axb.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fb.xy(3.0, yb - 6), fb.xy(0.2, yb - 7.5), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=9,
                              color=OC, lw=1.3, zorder=6))
draw_marker(axb, *map(float, fb.xy(30, yb)), "off", "K", fb.pts_per_yard())
for dy in (-12, -6, 0, 6, 12):
    draw_marker(axb, *map(float, fb.xy(70, yb + dy)), "off", "", fb.pts_per_yard())
band(fb, 90, 110, 0, FIELD_WIDTH, style.SERIES[2], alpha=0.12)
axb.text(*fb.xy(100, yb + 15.0), "landing\nzone", fontsize=6.4, ha="center", va="center", color=GREEN)
axb.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fb.xy(30, yb), fb.xy(100, yb - 4), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                              color=style.BALL, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 2)), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.12", zorder=6))
ret = 110 - int(S["sk_start"])
axb.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fb.xy(100, yb - 4), fb.xy(ret, yb - 4), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                              color=DC, lw=2.2, zorder=6))
axb.text(*fb.xy(12, yb - 12.0), "punter runs out of the\nend zone: 2 points,\nseconds off the clock", fontsize=6.6,
         ha="left", va="center", color=style.INK, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axb.text(*fb.xy(30, yb + 12.5), "safety kick\nfrom your 20", fontsize=6.6, ha="center", va="center", color=OC,
         zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axb.text(*fb.xy(70, yb + 16.2), "coverage lines up on the opponent's 40", fontsize=6.4, ha="center", va="center",
         color=OC, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axb.text(*fb.xy(ret + 9, yb - 12.0), f"returned to the opponent's\nown {S['sk_start']} (median)", fontsize=6.6,
         ha="center", va="center", color=DC, zorder=9, bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))
axb.set_title("B. Take the safety, then kick from the 20", loc="left", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2)
plt.show()
```

In field position alone, the swap is worth about `{python} S["safety_gain"]` yards, and it also
removes the chance of a blocked punt. The arithmetic only works with a lead of **three or more** (a safety must not tie the game) and when the
clock is nearly gone, so the opponent's drive after the kick is short. The best-known example is the
Ravens' in Super Bowl XLVII, covered in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd).
The boldest came earlier. On *Monday Night Football* in November 2003, Bill Belichick's Patriots trailed
Denver 24–23 with 2:51 left and fourth down at their own 1. Long snapper Lonie Paxton snapped the ball
through the end zone on purpose: 26–23 Broncos. The free kick from the 20 pushed Denver back to its own
15; New England used two timeouts to force a three-and-out, got the ball back at its own 42 after the
punt, and Brady threw the winning touchdown to David Givens with 36 seconds left.[^pats2003] Belichick
had paid two points to swap the worst field position in football for a defensive stand and a
short field. Modern teams use the simpler version in the final seconds: the Chiefs took one with 15
seconds left in a January 2025 divisional-round win over Houston, and the Eagles with six seconds left
against Tampa Bay in 2025.[^modernsafety]

#### Sidebar plate: the fair-catch kick

After any fair catch, the receiving team may choose a
[**fair-catch kick**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fair-catch-kick) instead of a snap: a place kick
(no tee) or a drop kick for three points, taken *from the spot of the catch*, with the defense lined up
ten yards away. There is no snap, no holder seven yards back, and no realistic rush. Two details make it
interesting. The kick is eight yards shorter than a field goal from the same line of scrimmage (spot plus
10 for the end zone, instead of plus 18), and the period can be **extended** for it: if time runs out
during the punt on which the fair catch is made, the receiving team may still take the kick.[^fckick]

```{python}
#| label: fig-fck-plate
#| fig-cap: "The fair-catch kick, as Cameron Dicker made it for the Chargers on December 19, 2024. Denver punted from deep in its own end with eight seconds left in the first half; the Chargers fair-caught the ball, and a 15-yard foul on the punting team for interfering with the fair catch moved the spot to the Denver 47 as time expired. The Chargers chose the fair-catch kick: the holder put the ball down at the 47 itself, the defense lined up 10 yards away, and Dicker's kick needed to travel 47 + 10 = 57 yards. A field goal from a snap at the same line would have been a 65-yarder."
fc = Field(orient="horizontal", los=63, window=(-14, 57), to_go=None, lateral=(12.0, 41.3), width_in=6.5)
ax = fc.ax
no_numbers(fc)
ppy = fc.pts_per_yard()
draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(63, MIDDLE)), "off", "H", ppy)
draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(60.6, MIDDLE + 1.4)), "off", "K", ppy)
for dy in (-7, -4.5, -2, 0.5, 3, 5.5, 8):
    draw_marker(ax, *map(float, fc.xy(73.6, MIDDLE + dy)), "def", "", ppy)
for x, c, lab in [(73, style.DEFENSE_DARK, "defense's line:\n10 yards away"), (55, style.MUTED, "where a holder would kneel\nfor a field goal from scrimmage")]:
    fc._line([x, x], [12.5, 41.0], color=c, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (4, 2)), zorder=2)
ax.text(*fc.xy(74.5, 16.0), "defense lines up\n10 yards away", fontsize=6.6, color=DC, ha="left", va="center",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"), zorder=9)
ax.text(*fc.xy(54.0, 16.5), "a field goal from a snap\nhere: 47 + 18 = 65 yards", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2,
        ha="right", va="center", bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"), zorder=9)
ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(fc.xy(63, MIDDLE), fc.xy(118.5, MIDDLE), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                             color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 2)), connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.12", zorder=6))
for dy in (-3.08, 3.08):                                      # goalposts on the end line
    fc._line([119.6, 119.6], [MIDDLE + dy - 0.1, MIDDLE + dy + 0.1], color=style.INK, lw=3)
fc._line([119.6, 119.6], [MIDDLE - 3.08, MIDDLE + 3.08], color=style.INK, lw=1.6)
ax.text(*fc.xy(88, 36.5), "fair catch, spotted at the DEN 47\nkick from the spot: 47 + 10 = 57 yards",
        fontsize=7, color=OC, ha="center", va="center", fontweight="bold",
        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6), zorder=9)
ax.text(*fc.xy(113.5, 37.0), "end line\nand posts", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center")
plt.show()
```

Dicker's 57-yarder was the first successful fair-catch kick in the NFL since 1976. Attempts are rare
because the circumstances are: the fair catch has to come near the end of a half (otherwise the team would
rather keep the drive alive) and close enough for a 55- to 65-yard kick. But with modern kickers making
long field goals routinely, coaches now keep it on the end-of-half card, and you should too. Watch for a
punt from deep in a team's own territory in the last ten seconds of a half: if the returner signals for
a fair catch near midfield, the kicking unit may run on with no snapper.

## Fourth down: the go-for-it decision

For most of NFL history, fourth down was a kicking down. Inside field-goal range you kicked; outside it
you punted; you went for it on fourth-and-inches near midfield, or when you were losing late. The
[**go-for-it decision**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-go-for-it-decision), the choice among going for
it, kicking and punting, has since become the most visible place where analytics changed football.

The argument is an expected-points argument, and you have the tools for it from
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd).
Take fourth-and-2 at the opponent's 36:

- **Punt**: the opponent takes over somewhere around its own 10, a situation worth a little to it.
  You've traded a scoring chance for field position.
- **Field goal**: a 54-yarder. Modern kickers make those about `{python} S["fg5054"]` of the time
  (2023–2025); a miss gives the opponent the ball at the spot of the kick, its own 44.
- **Go for it**: teams converted fourth-and-2 `{python} S["c2"]` of the time in 2021–2025. Success keeps
  a drive alive inside field-goal range; failure gives the opponent the ball at its own 36.

Put values on each outcome and the "go" option usually wins: the gain from converting (a drive that now
scores often) is bigger than the cost of failing (the opponent's field position is only somewhat
better than after a punt). The economist David Romer made exactly this case in a 2006 paper with a
mischievous title, "Do Firms Maximize? Evidence from Professional Football," and concluded that NFL teams
punted and kicked far more often than the numbers justified.[^romer] For a decade coaches mostly ignored
him. Then the data went public, a generation of analysts built fourth-down models (Ben Baldwin's open
model and its bot, which grades every fourth down live, is the best known), and teams hired their own
analysts.[^nfl4th] The modern decision tools use [**win probability**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-win-probability) (the chance of winning the game from
this score, clock and field position), not just expected points, so they know when the score makes a
field goal worth more than its three points. That model is built in
[Win Probability and Decision Analysis](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd);
this chapter sticks to what the decisions look like and why they changed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-go-rate
#| fig-cap: "How often NFL teams went for it on fourth down, 2010-2025 regular seasons: all fourth downs (punts, field-goal tries and plays that went for it, including fakes), and the neutral ones, in the first three quarters with each team's win probability between 20% and 80%, where the decision is a choice rather than desperation. The neutral rate hovered around 5-8% through 2017, climbed to about 15% by 2021, dipped in 2022-2023, and reached about 17% in 2025. Fourth downs wiped out by a pre-snap penalty are not counted. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.4))
for i, ccol in enumerate(GO.columns):
    ax.plot(GO.index, GO[ccol], color=style.SERIES[i], lw=2, marker="o", ms=3.5, label=ccol)
ax.axvspan(2017.5, 2025.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.35, zorder=0)
ax.text(2018.0, 0.012, "the aggression era", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="center")
for ccol, yy, off_ in [(GO.columns[0], GO.iloc[-1, 0], 0.012), (GO.columns[1], GO.iloc[-1, 1], -0.014)]:
    ax.text(2025.3, yy + off_, pct(yy), fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK, ha="right", va="center", fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlim(2009.6, 2025.6)
ax.set_ylim(0, 0.26)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(plt.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v:.0%}"))
ax.set_xticks(range(2010, 2026, 2))
ax.set_ylabel("Share of fourth downs: went for it")
ax.set_title("Fourth down stopped being a kicking down")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=7.5)
plt.show()
```

The neutral go rate more than doubled, from `{python} S["gon10"]` in 2010 and `{python} S["gon17"]` in 2017
to `{python} S["gon25"]` in 2025; across all fourth downs it went from `{python} S["go10"]` to
`{python} S["go25"]`. The turn came in 2018, the season after Doug Pederson's Eagles won a Super Bowl with
fourth-down conversions in the biggest moments, including the "Philly Special" touchdown on fourth-and-goal
in Super Bowl LII.[^philly] It is tempting to tell the story as one coach and one trick play. The truer story is the
slow arrival of evidence: public models, analysts on every staff, owners asking questions, and a
generation of head coaches who had grown up with the arguments.

Where did the extra attempts come from? Not from fourth-and-long in your own territory, which still
almost nobody tries. They came from short yardage around midfield, where teams used to punt, and from
short yardage inside field-goal range, where they used to kick. The fringe just outside kicking range,
which [Early Downs and Field Zones](10-01-early-downs-and-field-zones.qmd) calls
[**four-down territory**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-down-territory), already saw teams go on
fourth-and-1 and 2 a decade ago; the change there is on fourth-and-3, where the go rate roughly doubled.

```{python}
#| label: fig-go-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Go-for-it rate by yards to go and field position, first three quarters only (so that late-game desperation doesn't count), 2010-2012 versus 2023-2025 regular seasons. Each cell shows the share of fourth downs on which the offense went for it; cells with fewer than 15 fourth downs are left blank. The biggest changes are on short yardage (fourth-and-1 to 4) between your own 40 and the opponent's 40, and inside field-goal range, where fourth-and-1 and 2 used to mean a kick. The opponent's 30-39, too far for an easy kick and too close for a good punt, was already a go zone on fourth-and-1 a decade earlier. Fourth-and-long in your own half barely moved. Source: nflverse play-by-play."
from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
HM = f4[f4.qtr <= 3].copy()
HM["ytg"] = HM.ydstogo.clip(upper=10).astype(int)
ZEDGES = [0, 9, 19, 29, 39, 49, 59, 69, 79, 100]
ZLABS = ["opp\n1-9", "opp\n10-19", "opp\n20-29", "opp\n30-39", "opp\n40-49", "own\n41-50", "own\n31-40",
         "own\n21-30", "own\n1-20"]
HM["zone"] = pd.cut(HM.yardline_100, ZEDGES, labels=ZLABS)
cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("blues", ["#f4f8fd"] + style.SEQUENTIAL_BLUE)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.9), sharey=True)
for ax, (lo, hi) in zip(axes, [(2010, 2012), (2023, 2025)]):
    sub = HM[HM.season.between(lo, hi)]
    tab = sub.pivot_table(index="ytg", columns="zone", values="go", aggfunc="mean", observed=False)
    n = sub.pivot_table(index="ytg", columns="zone", values="go", aggfunc="size", observed=False)
    tab = tab.where(n >= 15)[ZLABS[::-1]]
    n = n[ZLABS[::-1]]
    ax.imshow(tab.values, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=0.9, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(tab.shape[0]):
        for j in range(tab.shape[1]):
            v = tab.values[i, j]
            if np.isfinite(v):
                ax.text(j, i, f"{100 * v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.3,
                        color="white" if v > 0.5 else style.INK)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(ZLABS)), ZLABS[::-1], fontsize=5.8)
    ax.set_yticks(range(10), [str(k) if k < 10 else "10+" for k in range(1, 11)], fontsize=7)
    ax.set_title(f"{lo}-{hi}", fontsize=9, loc="center")
    ax.grid(False)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)
axes[0].set_ylabel("Yards to go on fourth down")
fig.supxlabel("Ball on (offense moving left to right)", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
fig.suptitle("Go-for-it rate (%), first three quarters", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=10, fontweight="bold")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

### Fourth-down rules of thumb

You don't need a model to make a decent call from the couch. These heuristics agree with the public models
in most situations, for an average offense and kicker, with the score close and plenty of time left:

- **Fourth-and-1: go almost anywhere past your own 30**, and in many models even deeper. Teams converted
  `{python} S["c1"]` of fourth-and-1s in 2021–2025 (this includes the
  [QB sneak and tush push](10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd), which convert more often
  still).
- **Fourth-and-2 or 3: go from about midfield in.** Conversion rates were `{python} S["c2"]` and
  `{python} S["c3"]`.
- **The opponent's 30 to 40 is the "go zone."** It is too far for a sure field goal and too close for a
  good punt (a punt from the 35 nets only about 25 yards, and 15 if it bounces into the end zone), so even fourth-and-4 or 5 (converted
  `{python} S["c45"]`) is usually a go there.
- **Inside the opponent's 5: go on fourth-and-goal from the 1 or 2** unless the score says three points
  matter more than seven. A failed try still leaves the opponent pinned at its own goal line.
- **Long yardage in your own half: punt.** Fourth-and-6 to 10 converts only about `{python} S["c610"]` of
  the time, and failure gives the opponent a short field.
- **Then let the score and clock override everything.** Trailing late, go more; leading late, the value
  of the clock (and of making the opponent need two scores) can flip a go into a kick.

Two things these rules leave out are what make real decisions hard: **your** offense and kicker are not
average, and the opponent's offense matters (if they score at will, possessions are worth more, so go).
That's why two smart coaches can disagree about the same fourth down.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Going for it and failing proves it was the wrong call." A fourth-and-2 that converts 58% of the time
fails 42% of the time; a good decision loses a lot of coin flips. Judge the decision by the odds at the
moment it was made, not by the result, and judge a coach's fourth-down record by hundreds of decisions,
not by the one on Sunday night. (The reverse is also true: a punt that "worked" was not necessarily right.)
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Lions 2021-2025, Dan Campbell's fourth downs"}
No coach has been more associated with fourth-down aggression than Dan Campbell, hired by Detroit in 2021.
In the first three quarters of games from 2022 to 2025, the Lions went for it on `{python} S["det_go"]`
of their fourth downs, the highest rate in the league (the league average was `{python} S["lg_go"]`; next
were the `{python} S["team2"]` at `{python} S["team2_go"]`), and they led the league in that rate in
`{python} S["det_firsts"]` of the five seasons from 2021 to 2025.[^lions] Campbell made aggression part of
the team's identity from his first season, and for most of
those seasons the conversions and points it produced were part of why Detroit's offense was one of the
best in football.

The game everyone remembers went the other way. In the NFC Championship Game on January 28, 2024, at
San Francisco, Detroit led 24–7 at halftime. Midway through the third quarter, leading 24–10, the Lions went
for it on fourth-and-2 from the 49ers' 28, inside field-goal range, and threw incomplete. Late in the
game, trailing 27–24, they went for it on fourth-and-3 from the 30, again in range for a tying kick, and
threw incomplete again. San Francisco scored after both, and won 34–31.

What to notice: those were exactly the kind of calls the heuristics call close, a short fourth down at the
edge of field-goal range, with a strong kicker available. Reasonable people (and models) disagreed about
them before the snap; after the snap, the results made them look like blunders. The fair evaluation is the
whole record, and on the whole record Detroit's aggression was a net positive for years. The lesson for a
viewer is to separate the decision from the dice, and to notice that the most aggressive coach in the
league still faced exactly the trade-off this chapter describes, possessions against points, every week.
:::

## Two-point decisions and the two-point chart

After a touchdown the scoring team chooses between the
[extra point](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-extra-point) (a 33-yard kick since the league moved it back
in 2015) and a [two-point conversion](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-point-conversion) (one play
from the 2). Since 2015 the kick has been good `{python} S["xp_rate"]` of the time and the two-point try
has succeeded `{python} S["two_rate"]` of the time, so the expected points are almost the same:
`{python} S["xp_ev"]` for the kick, `{python} S["two_ev"]` for the try.[^twopoint] When two choices are
worth the same on average, **the score decides**. That's the job of the
[**two-point chart**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-point-chart): a table, keyed by the margin
right after the touchdown, of when two points are worth more than one. Coaches have carried versions of
it for half a century; the NFL added the two-point try in 1994.[^vermeil]

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-point-chart
#| fig-cap: "A simple two-point chart for late in a game, when only one or two more scores are likely. Find the margin right after the touchdown, before the try. 'Go' (blue) means two points turn the margin into a better number: tying (down 2), making a field goal enough to tie (down 5), keeping it a one-score game (down 10), or forcing the opponent to need more than one kind of score (up 1, 5 and 12). 'Kick' (grey) means the extra point is as good or better. 'Close' (yellow) cases depend on the time left and the two teams. Down 8, the most debated case, is explained in the text. Earlier in a game, kick unless you think your two-point play beats 50%."
CH = {-11: "K", -10: "G", -9: "C", -8: "G", -7: "K", -6: "K", -5: "G", -4: "C", -3: "K", -2: "G", -1: "C",
      1: "G", 2: "C", 3: "K", 4: "K", 5: "G", 6: "K", 7: "K", 8: "K", 9: "C", 10: "K", 11: "K", 12: "G",
      13: "K", 14: "K", 15: "G"}
FC = {"G": style.SERIES[0], "K": style.GRID, "C": "#f5cf6b"}
TC = {"G": "white", "K": style.INK, "C": style.INK}
WORD = {"G": "GO", "K": "kick", "C": "close"}
WHY = {-10: "→ down 8:\none score", -8: "see\ntext", -5: "→ down 3:\nFG ties", -2: "→ tie",
       1: "→ up 3:\nFG only ties", 5: "→ up 7:\nTD only ties", 12: "→ up 14:\nneeds 2 TDs", 15: "→ up 17:\n3 scores"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.6, 3.5))
for ax, rng, title in [(axes[0], range(-11, 0), "Trailing after the touchdown by"),
                       (axes[1], range(1, 16), "Leading after the touchdown by")]:
    blank(ax)
    keys = list(rng)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 15.6)
    ax.set_ylim(-1.9, 1.3)
    for i, m in enumerate(keys):
        c = CH[m]
        ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((i - 0.44, -0.4), 0.88, 0.95, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=0.12",
                                    fc=FC[c], ec="white", lw=1))
        ax.text(i, 0.25, f"{abs(m)}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", color=TC[c])
        ax.text(i, -0.17, WORD[c], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.4, color=TC[c])
        if m in WHY:
            ax.text(i, -0.95, WHY[m], ha="center", va="center", fontsize=5.6, color=style.INK_2, linespacing=1.05)
    ax.text(-0.5, 0.95, title, ha="left", va="center", fontsize=8.5, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK)
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.4)
plt.show()
```

The logic in each "go" box is the same: does two points move the margin across a line that matters? The
lines are the numbers the other team can reach in one possession, 3 (a field goal) and 7 or 8 (a
touchdown with a kick or a two-pointer).

The famous modern case is **trailing by 8 after a touchdown**, which happens when you were down 14 and
score. The traditional answer was "kick, cut it to 7, and hope for another touchdown and overtime." The
analytics answer is "go for two *now*." Make it (about half the time) and you trail by 6, so your next
touchdown and extra point win the game in regulation. Miss it and you trail by 8, so you need a touchdown
and a two-pointer to tie, but you *know* that now and can plan the rest of the game around it. Over the
two touchdowns, going early wins outright about half the time you get both scores and goes to overtime
some of the rest; kicking twice almost always goes to overtime, a coin flip. With a two-point success rate near 48%, going
early wins about 60% of the games in which you score both touchdowns, against about 50% for kicking, and it
also tells you before the last drive what you need.

Like the fourth-down rules, the chart assumes few scores remain. Early in a game, with many possessions
to come, the margin will change again before it matters, so teams simply take the better expected value,
which since 2015 has been close to a tie. A team with a great short-yardage offense (the Eagles of the
tush-push era, for example) should go for two more often than the chart says.

## Overtime

The [**overtime rules**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-overtime-rules) have changed more in the last
fifteen years than almost any other part of the game, and the reason is visible in one game. Under the old
sudden-death rule (in the regular season from 1974), the first team to score in overtime won. That gave a
big edge to the team that won the coin toss, and the edge grew as offenses improved. The league chipped
away at it: in 2010 (playoffs) and 2012 (regular season) a field goal on the first possession no longer
ended the game, but a touchdown still did; in 2017 regular-season overtime was cut from 15 minutes to
10.[^ot] Then came the January 2022 divisional-round game in Kansas City, the "thirteen seconds" game
covered in [The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd): the
Chiefs won the toss, drove for a touchdown, and Josh Allen never touched the ball. That spring the league
changed playoff overtime so that **both teams get a possession**. In 2025 it extended the rule to the
regular season.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ot-flow
#| fig-cap: "NFL overtime as of the 2026 season. A new coin toss; the winner usually chooses to receive or kick. Both teams are guaranteed one possession (the kickoff itself counts as the receiving team's chance), except that a safety by the kicking team on the first possession ends the game. After both have had the ball, the team ahead wins; if it is still tied, the next score of any kind wins. The regular season and the playoffs differ in what happens when time runs out: the regular season has one 10-minute period and can end in a tie (two timeouts each), while the playoffs play as many 15-minute periods as needed (three timeouts per 'half' of two periods)."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.6))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0, 78)
box(ax, 50, 73, 58, 7, "Tied after four quarters: new coin toss", ec=style.INK_2, bold=True, fs=8.5)
box(ax, 50, 59.5, 62, 10, "Team A's first possession", sub="(the team that receives the kickoff)",
    fs=8.3, sub_fs=6.8)
arrow(ax, (50, 69.4), (50, 64.6))
box(ax, 10, 44.5, 19, 10.5, "B's defense\nscores a safety", sub="Team B wins", fs=7.2, sub_fs=7.0,
    fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
arrow(ax, (30, 54.4), (12, 49.8))
box(ax, 60.5, 44.5, 76, 10.5, "Team B gets its possession, whatever Team A did",
    sub="A scored a TD: B needs a TD to tie (or a TD plus a two-pointer to win at once).\nA kicked a FG: B needs a FG to tie, a TD wins.   A didn't score: any score by B wins.",
    fs=7.6, sub_fs=6.2)
arrow(ax, (57, 54.4), (57, 49.8))
box(ax, 57, 29, 70, 9, "Both have had the ball: ahead wins; tied, the next score wins",
    fs=7.6, ec=style.INK_2)
arrow(ax, (57, 39.2), (57, 33.6))
box(ax, 30, 11.5, 40, 13, "Regular season", sub="one 10-minute period\n2 timeouts each\nstill tied at 0:00: a tie",
    fs=8, sub_fs=6.6, fc=MAYBE_C, ec="#c99a00", bold=True)
box(ax, 74, 11.5, 40, 13, "Playoffs", sub="15-minute periods until\nsomeone wins; 3 timeouts\nper two periods",
    fs=8, sub_fs=6.6, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, bold=True)
arrow(ax, (45, 24.4), (33, 18.2))
arrow(ax, (69, 24.4), (72, 18.2))
ax.text(51, 21.5, "if the clock\nruns out", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center", linespacing=1.05)
plt.show()
```

The details are in the rulebook's Rule 16; the strategy follows from three facts.[^otrule]

**Second possession is information.** The team that gets the ball second knows exactly what it needs. If the
first team kicked a field goal, the second can use all four downs in its own territory, because a punt is
no longer an option worth taking. If the first team scored a touchdown, the second must too, and then
decide whether to kick and play on or go for two and win on the spot.

**First possession is a potential third possession.** If the game is still tied after both teams have had
the ball, the next score wins, and the team that received first is the one most likely to get the ball
next. In the playoffs, with unlimited time, that potential third possession has real value; in the
regular season's 10-minute period, it often never comes.

**The clock is a weapon in the regular season.** Ten minutes is short. A first team that drives slowly for
a field goal can leave the second team with four or five minutes and the need for points; a long drive
by the second team can run the clock out, and the game ends in a tie.

That is why there's no consensus on whether to receive. Analytics researchers still tend to find a
small edge in **receiving**, mostly because of that possible third possession; many coaches and former
players on television prefer **kicking off**, for the information and the free use of fourth down. The
edge either way is small, it depends on the two offenses, and the regular season's 10-minute clock makes
the third possession less likely.[^otchoice]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs 2023 season — Super Bowl LVIII overtime"}
Super Bowl LVIII was the first Super Bowl played under the 2022 playoff overtime rule (and only the second
to reach overtime at all, after LI). After Butker's tying kick (see the timeline earlier in the chapter),
San Francisco won the coin toss and chose to **receive**. It drove from its own 25 to the Kansas City 9
over more than seven minutes and kicked a 27-yard field goal: 22–19.

Now Kansas City knew everything. A field goal would tie and send the game to sudden death; a touchdown
would win. On fourth-and-1 at its own 34, with the season on the line, the Chiefs went for it (a punt
would have meant that any San Francisco score won the game), and Mahomes ran for eight yards. On
third-and-1 at the 49ers' 32 he scrambled for 19 more. The drive ended with a three-yard touchdown pass to
Mecole Hardman with three seconds left in the first overtime period: 25–22, Kansas City.

What to notice: the 49ers' choice to receive, debated for weeks afterwards, followed the old sudden-death
instinct. Under the new rule a first-possession touchdown no longer ends the game, so receiving first mainly
bought San Francisco a *possible* third possession; it also meant the 49ers drove without knowing what
they needed, and settled for three points. Deferring would have handed that information to them. Notice too how the
second team plays four-down football from its own 34: the rule changed what fourth down means.
:::

## Film room: the clock manager's reputation

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs 2015 season — the slow drive at Foxborough"}
Andy Reid is now remembered for one of the best two-minute offenses in football, but for most of his
career "clock management" was the phrase his critics reached for. The two examples you'll hear most:

- **Super Bowl XXXIX (2004 season).** Reid's Eagles trailed New England 24–14 with 5:40 left and the
  ball. They drove for a touchdown, but the drive took 3:52 of clock, with the clock running between many
  of the snaps, and the Eagles held two timeouts the entire way. They scored with 1:48 left, failed on the
  onside kick, and got the ball back only at their own 4 with 46 seconds left.
- **AFC Divisional Round, January 16, 2016 (2015 season).** Reid's Chiefs trailed the Patriots 27–13 and
  took over at their own 20 with 6:29 left. The touchdown came with 1:13 left: a 16-play drive that used
  **5:16**, with the clock running between many of the snaps and all three timeouts unused. The
  onside kick failed, and New England knelt out the game.[^reid]

What to notice: both drives *scored*. The problem was the price. Trailing by two scores, a team needs
two possessions, and the second one has to come from the time the first one leaves. In the price list
from the top of the chapter, the difference between huddling (40-odd seconds a play) and hurrying (about
20) over 13 or 16 plays is four or five minutes, roughly the time the second possession needed.

The postscript is the more interesting part. The Chiefs of the Mahomes era made the clock their weapon:
the thirteen-seconds game, the Super Bowl LVIII regulation drive charted above, and a long run of
end-of-half scores. The coach was the same; the quarterback, the play design, and the team's investment in
game management were not. Reputations in this area lag reality by years in both directions.
:::

## Coach the clock: one flowchart

Everything above compresses into a handful of questions a team asks after every play in the last two
minutes. The chart below is the version to keep in your head on Sunday.

```{python}
#| label: fig-clock-flow
#| fig-cap: "A clock decision flowchart for the last two minutes of a half. Left: the team with the ball needs points and time. After each play, first ask whether the clock is running; if it is, decide how much the next snap is worth and choose the cheapest stoppage that gets it (a hurry-up snap, a spike that spends a down, or a timeout that spends a timeout). Right: the team with the lead and the ball spends time instead, and the trailing defense's main tools are its timeouts (or, when it is behind by more than a score with time running out, letting the offense score to get the ball back). The bottom row is the end of the line: kneel when the arithmetic works, take the field goal with the clock stopped, or throw the Hail Mary when there is only one snap left."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 6.0))
blank(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_ylim(0, 100)
# left lane: trailing, with the ball
ax.text(25, 97.5, "TRAILING, WITH THE BALL", ha="center", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=OC)
ax.text(75, 97.5, "LEADING, WITH THE BALL", ha="center", fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=DC)
box(ax, 25, 88, 44, 7, "After the play: is the clock running?", bold=True, fs=7.6, ec=style.INK_2)
box(ax, 10, 75, 18, 9, "No", sub="incomplete or out\nof bounds (late)", fs=7.6, sub_fs=6.2, fc=STOP_C,
    ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, bold=True)
box(ax, 36, 75, 26, 9, "Yes", sub="tackled in bounds", fs=7.6, sub_fs=6.2, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, bold=True)
arrow(ax, (18, 84.4), (12, 79.7))
arrow(ax, (32, 84.4), (35, 79.7))
box(ax, 10, 59, 18, 13, "Take your time:\ncall two plays", sub="the clock starts\non the snap", fs=7.0,
    sub_fs=6.2)
arrow(ax, (10, 70.4), (10, 65.6))
box(ax, 35, 61.5, 29, 8, "Seconds left vs.\nplays needed?", fs=6.8, ec=style.INK_2)
arrow(ax, (36, 70.4), (36, 65.6))
box(ax, 24.5, 46, 17, 13, "Plenty", sub="hurry up, run a\nreal play\n(≈21 s)", fs=7.0, sub_fs=6.0)
box(ax, 42.5, 46, 16, 13, "Tight", sub="spike (≈16 s,\nspends a down)\nor timeout", fs=7.0, sub_fs=6.0)
arrow(ax, (32, 57.4), (26, 52.6))
arrow(ax, (40, 57.4), (42, 52.6))
box(ax, 25, 25, 46, 15, "In range with seconds left?",
    sub="get the clock stopped (spike or timeout),\nthen the field goal unit runs on.\nOne snap left, out of range: Hail Mary.",
    fs=7.4, sub_fs=6.2, ec=style.INK_2, bold=True)
arrow(ax, (25, 39.4), (25, 32.6), ls=(0, (3, 2)))
# right lane: leading, with the ball
box(ax, 75, 88, 44, 7, "Make every snap cost the most clock", bold=True, fs=7.6, ec=style.INK_2)
box(ax, 75, 73, 44, 13, "Run inside, stay in bounds,\nsnap with the play clock at 1",
    sub="a first down is worth about two minutes", fs=7.2, sub_fs=6.2)
arrow(ax, (75, 84.4), (75, 79.6))
box(ax, 75, 54.5, 44, 13, "Can three kneels end it?",
    sub="about 2:03 with no defensive timeouts;\nsubtract ≈40 s per timeout (and for the\ntwo-minute warning, if it's still to come)",
    fs=7.2, sub_fs=6.0, ec=style.INK_2, bold=True)
arrow(ax, (75, 66.4), (75, 61.1))
box(ax, 64, 37, 20, 10, "Yes:\nvictory formation", fs=7.0, fc=RUN_C, ec=GREEN, bold=True)
box(ax, 87, 37, 22, 10, "No: keep running,\nfirst downs end it", fs=7.0, fc=STOP_C, ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
arrow(ax, (70, 47.9), (65, 42.1))
arrow(ax, (80, 47.9), (85, 42.1))
ax.text(75, 23.5, "MEANWHILE, THE TRAILING DEFENSE", ha="center", fontsize=7, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK_2)
box(ax, 75, 14, 44, 13, "Use the timeouts early",
    sub="timeout right after each in-bounds run;\nlate, still behind by more than a score?\nlet them score, get the ball back",
    fs=7.4, sub_fs=6.0, fc=MAYBE_C, ec="#c99a00", bold=True)
ax.plot([50, 50], [3, 95], color=style.GRID, lw=1.2, zorder=0)
plt.show()
```

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: coach the clock"}
**In the last two minutes of each half, call the clock decision before the team makes it.** Keep three
numbers in your head from the score bug: time left, each team's timeouts, and the yard line versus
field-goal range (add 18).

- **After every play, say "running" or "stopped"** before the broadcast tells you, and remember the
  out-of-bounds rule only bites after the first-half two-minute warning and in the last five minutes.
- **Trailing offense, clock running:** predict hurry-up, spike or timeout. Spike on first or second down
  with time for more plays; timeout when there's time for only one or two, or when the kicking unit has to
  come on.
- **Watch the receivers' feet.** On a sideline catch, does he get out, or turn upfield for two more yards?
  Did the defender push him out (a gift) or tackle him in bounds (a win for the defense)?
- **Leading team with a first down:** do the kneel math (about 2:03 with no defensive timeouts, 40 seconds
  less per timeout). If it works, call the victory formation before it lines up.
- **Trailing defense:** predict when it calls timeouts. A good one calls them right after the leading
  team's first-down and second-down runs, not at the end.
- **Fourth down before the snap:** go, kick or punt? Use the heuristics: fourth-and-1 almost always go;
  opponent's 30 to 40 is the go zone; long yardage in your own half, punt.
- **After a touchdown late:** find the margin and check the two-point chart (down 2, 5, 8 or 10; up 1, 5
  or 12: expect them to go).
- **At the end of the first half:** who receives the second-half kickoff? That team will push harder for a
  late score.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: spike or snap?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-spike
#| fig-cap: "Fourth quarter, 0:31 and running. The offense trails 20-18 and has no timeouts. It just completed a 12-yard pass to the opponent's 26 (first-and-10), and the receiver was tackled in bounds; the offense is sprinting back to the line. Its kicker is good from about 50 yards. A field goal from here would be a 44-yarder."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
p1 = Play(off, defense("nickel", "two_high", off), los=84, to_go=10)
fld = p1.draw(window=(-10, 21.5), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.985, 0.225, ["Q4  0:31 (running)", "AWAY 18   HOME 20", "1st & 10   ball on HOME 26",
                                "AWAY timeouts: 0"], fs=6.4, ha="right")
say(fld, p1, -6.5, -13.0, "offense hurrying\nto the line", color=OC, fs=6.6)
say(fld, p1, 17.5, 0.0, "a field goal from here: 26 + 18 = 44 yards", color=style.INK, fs=6.8, box_ec=style.BASELINE)
plt.show()
```

**Spike now, or snap a real play? And what has to be true before the field goal?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Spike, then take one quick shot toward the sideline, then kick with the clock stopped.** The key fact is
the one at the end of the question: **the field-goal unit realistically can't run on and set up while the
clock is running**, and with no timeouts the only ways to stop it are an incompletion, getting out of bounds, or a spike. So the
offense must not let a play end in bounds without a plan.

Price the options. Lining up and spiking costs about `{python} S["p_spike"]` seconds from the last snap,
counting from the completion's snap a few seconds before 0:31, so the clock stops at about 0:20 and it's
second-and-10. That leaves time for one more snap
that ends with the clock stopped (an out route or a throwaway), and then the kick. Running a real play
instead is a gamble: a catch in bounds at, say, the 18 would leave the offense needing to spike with the
clock still running and perhaps ten seconds left, which is fine; a sack or a run stuffed in bounds would
end the game. Coaches with no timeouts take the cheap, certain stoppage first. (If the offense *had* a
timeout, it would save it for the kick and still spike now.)
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: can they kneel it out?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-kneel
#| fig-cap: "Fourth quarter, 1:40 and running, after a first-down run. The offense leads 24-20 with first-and-10 at its own 35, and is jogging back to the line with a fresh 40-second play clock. The defense has one timeout left. The two-minute warning has already passed."
pk = Play(vf, vd, los=45, to_go=10)
fld = pk.draw(window=(-16.5, 12.5), lateral=(-19, 19), title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.985, 0.36, ["Q4  1:40 (running)", "HOME 24   AWAY 20", "1st & 10   ball on HOME 35",
                               "AWAY timeouts: 1"], fs=6.4, ha="right")
say(fld, pk, 9.0, 12.5, "defense: one\ntimeout left", color=DC, fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Can the offense kneel three times and end the game? What should the defense do with its timeout?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Yes: three kneels end it, and the timeout can't stop that.** Work the arithmetic from the kneel chart.
Kneel 1: the offense lets the play clock run, snaps at about 1:01 and the kneel ends at about 0:59. The
defense calls its timeout. Kneel 2 starts the clock on the snap and ends at about 0:57. With no timeouts
left, the play clock runs again: kneel 3 at about 0:18, ending around 0:16. Now it's fourth down with 16
seconds left and a 40-second play clock, so the game clock reaches zero before the offense has to snap
again. Game over, without a fourth-down play.

That's why the chart says one timeout is worth only about 40 seconds: the defense needed **two** timeouts
here (or the two-minute warning still to come) to force a fourth-down snap. It doesn't matter when it calls
the one it has; any order gives the same arithmetic. Its only real hope is a fumbled snap, which is exactly
what the victory formation, drawn here, is built to prevent.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: fourth-and-2 at the 36"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-fourth
#| fig-cap: "Second quarter, 6:00 left, tied 10-10. The offense faces fourth-and-2 at the opponent's 36 (yellow line: the line to gain). It has kept its regular 11-personnel offense on the field; the defense is in its nickel package with a two-high shell. A field goal from here would be a 54-yarder; the kicker's career long is 55."
off = offense("gun_2x2")
p3 = Play(off, defense("nickel", "two_high", off), los=74, to_go=2)
fld = p3.draw(window=(-10, 17), lateral="full", title=False)
no_numbers(fld)
scorebug(fld.ax, 0.985, 0.265, ["Q2  6:00", "HOME 10   AWAY 10", "4th & 2   ball on AWAY 36",
                               "FG: 36 + 18 = 54 yards"], fs=6.4, ha="right")
say(fld, p3, 3.6, 21.0, "line to gain", color="#9a6a00", fs=6.6)
plt.show()
```

**Punt, kick or go? What does the offense's personnel tell you about the decision it has already made?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Go for it, and the offense has told you so by leaving its offense on the field.** By every rule of thumb
in the chapter, this is a go: fourth-and-2 converts about `{python} S["c2"]` of the time; the 36 is in the
opponent's 30-to-40 "go zone", where a punt nets only about 25 yards and a 54-yard kick near this kicker's
limit misses often (the league made 50- to 54-yarders `{python} S["fg5054"]` of the time in 2023–2025,
and a kicker near his career long will do worse) and hands the opponent the ball at its own 44. In
2023–2025, teams in the first three quarters went for it on `{python} S["go_4th2_opp"]` of
fourth-and-2s between the opponent's 31 and 40, against `{python} S["go_4th2_old"]` in 2013–2015.

The pre-snap clue is the personnel: no punter or kicker jogging on, the regular offense lined up with the
quarterback in the shotgun. Some teams line up to go and then take a delay-of-game penalty or call a
timeout if they can't draw the defense offside, so wait for the snap; but a team that keeps 11 personnel on
the field on fourth-and-2 has made its decision on the sideline. As for the play: expect a quick pass or a
run that needs only 2 yards, from the short-yardage menu in
[Red Zone, Goal Line, Two-Point Plays, and Short Yardage](10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **The clock is a currency.** Late in a half the trailing team wants plays per second and the leading team
  wants seconds per play. Price every play: an incompletion or a catch out of bounds costs about
  `{python} S["p_inc"]`–`{python} S["p_oob"]` seconds, a catch in bounds about `{python} S["p_hurry"]`,
  unless a spike (a down) or a timeout pays for it.
- **Out of bounds stops the clock until the snap only late**: after the two-minute warning of the first
  half and in the last five minutes of the game. The **10-second runoff** punishes an offense that stops
  the clock illegally, and can end a half.
- **The two-minute drill** throws outside, avoids sacks, spikes on early downs and saves timeouts for the
  end. **The four-minute offense** does the opposite: runs inside, snaps at the end of the play clock, and
  treats first downs, not points, as the goal. Three kneels drain about two minutes, minus about 40 seconds
  per defensive timeout.
- **End-of-half calls** weigh points against the risk of a short field for the opponent. The **prevent
  defense** is right only when the clock makes yards cheap; the **Hail Mary** scores about one time in
  seventeen. The **intentional safety** and **fair-catch kick** are rare but decide games.
- **Fourth down became a decision**: the neutral go rate more than doubled from 2017 to 2025. Fourth-and-1
  is almost always a go, the opponent's 30–40 is the go zone, and good decisions still fail often.
- **Two points and overtime follow the score.** The two-point chart asks whether two points cross a line
  that matters (down 2, 5, 8, 10; up 1, 5, 12). Overtime gives both teams a possession; the second team
  plays with information, the first with a possible third possession.

[^modernsafety]: nflverse play-by-play: game `2024_20_HOU_KC` (January 18, 2025), "(Punt formation) 14-M.Araiza right end ran ob in End Zone for -18 yards, SAFETY" at 0:15 with Kansas City leading by 11; game `2025_04_PHI_TB`, "(Punt formation) 10-B.Mann right end tackled in End Zone for -34 yards, SAFETY" at 0:06 with Philadelphia leading by 8. The field-position comparison in the plate is a course calculation from 2015–2025 regular seasons: punts from the punting team's 1- to 4-yard line (n = `{python} S["ezp_n"]`) and free kicks from the 20 after a safety (n = `{python} S["sk_n"]`), taking the yard line of the receiving team's first snap; the safety-kick rules are NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 6, Section 1, Articles 1(b) and 2 (a safety kick may be a punt, drop kick or place kick, from the kicking team's 20, with the kicking team's other players on the receiving team's 40), and Rule 6, Section 2, Article 4 (a safety kick out of bounds or short of the landing zone gives the receiving team the ball 30 yards from the spot of the kick).

[^fckick]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 10, Section 2, Article 4 (after a fair catch the receiving team may put the ball in play "by a snap or fair catch kick (drop kick or place kick without a tee) from the spot of the catch"); Rule 11, Section 4, Article 3 (the receiving team's line is 10 yards in advance of the kick; onside-kick formation rules apply); Rule 4, Section 8, Article 2(e)–(f) (the period may be extended for a fair-catch kick). The Dicker kick: nflverse play-by-play, game `2024_16_DEN_LAC` (Dec. 19, 2024): the Denver punt fair-caught at the Chargers' 38 with 0:08 left, fair-catch interference enforced 15 yards, and "11-C.Dicker 57 yard field goal is GOOD ... Fair-Catch Kick" at 0:00; Kris Rhim, "'Ain't ever seen that': Rare fair catch kick propels Chargers," ESPN (Dec. 20, 2024; the last successful one was Ray Wersching's for San Diego in 1976): https://africa.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/43068684/obscure-rule-leads-chargers-making-nfl-first-fair-catch-kick-1976 . Unsuccessful attempts in the play-by-play include Phil Dawson's 71-yarder for San Francisco (2013) and Joey Slye's 60-yarder for Carolina (2019).

[^twopoint]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play, 2015–2025 regular seasons (`extra_point_result`, `two_point_conv_result`). See [Field Goals, Extra Points, and the Punting Game](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd) for the 2015 rule.

[^ot]: NFL Football Operations, "Overtime rules" and "Featured rules" (2025 regular-season change; 2022 playoff change after the January 2022 Bills–Chiefs game; 10-minute regular-season period since 2017): https://operations.nfl.com/rules-officiating/featured-rules ; the history (sudden death in the regular season from 1974; the modified rule in the 2010 playoffs and 2012 regular season): "Overtime (sports): American football," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtime_(sports)#American_football ; the 2017 cut to 10 minutes was approved by the owners on May 23, 2017: NFL.com, "NFL owners approve shortening overtime to 10 minutes": https://www.nfl.com/news/nfl-owners-approve-shortening-overtime-to-10-minutes-0ap3000000810488

[^otrule]: NFL Rulebook (2026), Rule 16, Section 1: Article 3 (regular season: one 10-minute period, both teams must have the opportunity to possess unless the kicking team scores a safety on the receiving team's first possession, two timeouts each, a tie if still level), Article 4 (postseason: 15-minute periods until there is a winner, three timeouts per half), Article 5(c) (the kickoff is the receiving team's opportunity to possess) and 5(d) (no coaches' challenges; the replay official starts all reviews).

[^otchoice]: David K. Li, "The NFL's overtime can still come down to a coin toss. Is it better to kick or receive?" NBC News (September 20, 2025): Ron Yurko of Carnegie Mellon's Sports Analytics Center, "I would take the ball, at least that's what the current evidence suggests," an edge "smaller than it was" under sudden death; NBC's Chris Simms and Fox's Greg Olsen favouring kicking off: https://www.nbcnews.com/sports/nfl/nfls-overtime-can-still-come-coin-toss-better-kick-receive-rcna231812
